chapters.title: Chapter 610: The Door to Jade Moon
paragraphs: She offered no details, and Leon did not press.
Her attention had already shifted to the estate.

The outer formations had been altered since her departure. The rear garden entrance was barred, and the guards beside it watched every approaching servant. A storehouse near the eastern wall stood empty. Damage had been cleaned, but not completely concealed from someone who knew what to look for.
"Someone entered this compound," Qingyue said.
"Four people," Yanning replied. "All Void Immortals."
Qingyue turned toward her. Surprise crossed her face, then disappeared beneath focused attention.

They met Shen Yuanhe in the private room beside the family court. The old man summarized the attack himself: four intruders, three permanent deaths, one captured leader, a tracking formation placed on the treasure before delivery, and a local observer manipulated into sending a false success report.
Qingyue listened without interrupting.
"How long will the tracker’s suppression remain believable?" she asked when he finished.
"A few days," Leon said.
"When is the next expected contact?"
"The prisoners gave us a range, not an exact hour. We’re keeping them separate and comparing everything else they say."
"Did the local agent transmit anything before the false report?"
"He began writing a failure report, then burned it after receiving the authenticated message. I waited until his replacement transmission was complete before taking him."
Qingyue gave a small nod. "Good. If you had interrupted it halfway, the receiving jade might have recorded the failure."
"That was my concern."
"Show me the Void Immortal."
They descended to the strongroom. Qingyue stood before the captured leader and extended her senses toward Leon’s restraint without touching it.

The spatial fold did not treat the Ethereal foundation as a nearby object. It controlled the routes through which the prisoner’s manifestation could access that distributed foundation. He remained whole and capable of surviving, but unable to escape through reformation.
Qingyue studied the structure for several breaths.
"You can restrain his connection without damaging the foundation," she said after they returned to the yard.
"Yes."
"Several elders in Jade Moon Palace could do the same. Most Void Immortals could not." Her eyes rested on him briefly. "That explains why he chose to bargain."
She also recognized the notched iron ring.

"Ninefold Ridge is dangerous," she said. "The Qiao clan has no direct dispute with Jade Moon Palace, and the Palace will not begin a regional conflict over an attempted theft from a merchant family. I can confirm what the mark means. I cannot make the clan disappear."
"We didn’t expect you to," Yanning said.
"Good. The false report was the right choice, but it will expire. When the promised contact fails and the treasure never arrives, Ninefold Ridge will send someone more cautious than the first group."
Shen Yuanhe nodded. "We intend to use the time."

Qingyue did not offer an easy solution because none existed. She gave Yanning two names of neutral formation masters who did not work for the city’s four houses, then left the family to continue its preparations.
Less than an hour after her arrival, she and Leon stood on the western wall as sunset colored Moonfall’s roofs.
"You promised me a surprise," Leon said.
"I did."
Qingyue rested one hand on the parapet and looked across the northern quarter. Ore lifts moved between towers while evening lanterns came alive below them.
"Part of the surprise depended on whether you were still here," she said.
"You were testing me?"
"I was checking my judgment. We spent roughly four days close together. That was enough to form an opinion, but not enough to trust it completely."
She turned toward him.

"You could have left Moonfall, taken work in the Desolation, or attached yourself to one of the city’s major houses. Instead, you stayed in a merchant family’s guest wing, learned what ordinary food cost, and protected an old man’s refinement from four Void Immortals."
"I didn’t do that to impress you."
"I know. That makes the decision more useful."
Qingyue straightened.

"Jade Moon Palace is a major sect of the Eastern Jade Sea," she said. "Its archives contain cultivation paths Moonfall’s markets will never sell. Its training grounds, teachers, and private resources draw talented cultivators from across the region. It is the kind of place you have been trying to reach without knowing its name."

She described it without ceremony. The Palace held territories across the islands of the Eastern Jade Sea and drew candidates from far beyond Moonfall. New arrivals did not train beside core disciples or receive rare inheritances merely because they passed through the gate. They were assessed and placed according to talent, cultivation, conduct, and what the sect believed they could become.
"A recommendation means they will not dismiss you as an unknown wanderer with no lineage record," Qingyue said. "It ensures the recruitment elders examine you seriously. Nothing more."
Leon remained quiet.
"I am willing to recommend you as a recruitment candidate."
"On what grounds?"

"Four rare affinities with enough range to support one another. Precise control. A clean foundation and no sign of corruption or demonic cultivation. More importantly, you remain calm when a bad decision would be easier."
She raised a hand before he could answer.

"My recommendation opens the gate. It does not carry you through the assessment. The Palace will examine you, test you, and decide for itself. Several disciples and true heirs in my generation are stronger than you in an open fight, and the sect has no shortage of talented candidates. You may be rejected."
"And if I refuse?"
"Then you refuse. This is not repayment for anything that happened in the Desolation. You owe me and the Palace nothing."
"Would your recommendation make you responsible for me?"

"Only for bringing you to their attention in good faith. If you lie during the assessment, attack someone, or prove unsuitable, the consequences are yours." A faint edge of humor entered her voice. "I am offering an introduction, Leon. I am not adopting you."
Leon looked out over the city.

A major sect offered the knowledge he had spent the last six days gathering one fragment at a time. Its archives might explain this world’s cultivation, its higher ranks, and which resources could benefit the people living inside his dimensional world.
It also meant scrutiny.
Jade Moon Palace would notice that he possessed no normal spiritual root or recognizable circulation method. A serious assessment might discover far more than a market examination ever could.
But remaining ignorant is its own danger.
The Trial Overseer still existed somewhere far above this frontier city. Leon could not prepare for that threat with beginner manuals and guesses.
"When would we leave?" he asked.

"Not tonight, and not tomorrow," Qingyue replied. "The Shens need time to move their vulnerable assets, and both prisoners may still give you useful information. Finish what you need to finish. I will wait."

Below them, fresh guards took their positions around the inner estate. The Qiao clan’s threat had been delayed, not ended. Leon now had access to the Shen trade network, a living resource Loriel might propagate, and an opportunity that could carry him beyond Moonfall.
Qingyue extended one hand, palm upward in the formal manner of this world.
"Come with me to Jade Moon Palace. I cannot promise they will accept you, but I can make certain they look."
Leon glanced once toward the guarded rear estate, then met her eyes.
"That is enough."

Her attention had already shifted to the estate.
The outer formations had been altered since her departure.
The rear garden entrance was barred, and the guards beside it watched every approaching servant.
A storehouse near the eastern wall stood empty.
Damage had been cleaned, but not completely concealed from someone who knew what to look for.
"Someone entered this compound," Qingyue said.
"Four people," Yanning replied.
"All Void Immortals."
Qingyue turned toward her.
Surprise crossed her face, then disappeared beneath focused attention.
They met Shen Yuanhe in the private room beside the family court.

The old man summarized the attack himself: four intruders, three permanent deaths, one captured leader, a tracking formation placed on the treasure before delivery, and a local observer manipulated into sending a false success report.
Qingyue listened without interrupting.

"A few days," Leon said.
"When is the next expected contact?"

"That was my concern."

That was enough to form an opinion, but not enough to trust it completely."
She turned toward him.

"I didn’t do that to impress you."
"I know.
That makes the decision more useful."

She described it without ceremony.

Nothing more."

Precise control.
A clean foundation and no sign of corruption or demonic cultivation.

You may be rejected."
"And if I refuse?"

This is not repayment for anything that happened in the Desolation.
You owe me and the Palace nothing."

chapters.title: Chapter 611: The Enemies They Left Free
paragraphs: The Shen estate had not slept. From the street, it looked like a house that had.

Kitchen fires lit at the usual hour. The western yard opened for the dyers’ cart. Two clerks argued about a shortfall in the herb ledger loudly enough for the neighbors to hear, because silence would have been more interesting.
Leon came down to the cellar at first light with Yanning and the old man, and they took the local agent first.

He had spent a day sealed in a room with no idea what had happened to anyone else, and had used it to build a story. It was decent. He gave up a rented loft above a leatherworker’s in the sixth ward and swore the drops were made there. He gave up two names that turned out to belong to dead men. He described a courier route through the fish market on alternate days.

"The loft’s empty," Yanning said when he finished. "Two years now. My uncle looked at it for a bonded store and passed because the roof leaks. And the fish market closes at the second mark on the days you named, so there’s no through-traffic — you’d be a man standing alone among the stalls." She turned a page on her writing board. "Try again."
They went at it for two hours, and Leon never touched him.

What broke the agent was arithmetic. Leon had his movements from the paired device and from watching him personally. Shen Yuanhe had obtained the Void Immortal’s account of the contact protocol from the strongroom two floors away. Each time the agent’s story failed to line up, Yanning showed him where. He repaired it four times. On the fifth, he stopped and put his forehead against the wall.
What came out was smaller and far more useful than the loft.

A counting office on Redgate Lane that took commissions on grain contracts and kept a clean twelve-year book. A rented storehouse near the northern water gate holding equipment, communication tokens, and nothing worth stealing. Two couriers who believed they carried letters for a merchant house out of Baihe and had never heard the name Qiao. And one senior handler — the agent called him onlythe accountant— who knew exactly who paid him and was waiting for the raid team to surface.
"Strength?" Leon asked.
"The accountant’s the strongest. An Archon, I think, or close to it. The rest of us are nothing." The agent laughed once, badly. "We’re bookkeepers. They don’t send us anywhere."
Upstairs, Yanning laid it out on the table and reached for a pen.
"Redgate Lane, the storehouse, both couriers, the accountant. We can have all five before noon. My father has guards, you’re worth six of them, and the old man—"
"No," said Shen Yuanhe.
She stopped.

"Think about the day after," Leon said. "Ninefold Ridge believes its team walked out of here with the treasure and went to ground. Now every contact it has in Moonfall disappears in the same morning." He shook his head. "Nobody loses a whole network to coincidence. The report becomes a lie the moment we do that, and whoever they send next comes prepared for the first team to be dead."
Yanning put the pen down.
"A trusted channel is more useful to us than five prisoners," her great-grandfather said. "We watch them. We do not touch them."
So they built the other half of it instead.

Trusted factors got quiet standing instructions — a man to sit in the teahouse across from the Redgate counting office and buy nothing important, two guards rotating past the northern storehouse on a delivery route that already existed, someone to follow each courier without being told why. Yanning made a point of that last part.
Then they began feeding it.

A Shen factor, with a compromised courier standing four paces off, complained to a colleague that the family’s great purchase wasgoneand nobody upstairs would say where. He complained in the aggrieved tone of a man who had been shouted at that morning, then shut up too fast, the way a man does when he remembers himself.

A wagon left by the treasure delivery route with an empty bed and six guards riding out beside it, and came back at dusk with the guards filthy and short-tempered. One of them kicked the wheel before he went in.
A rumor went out on one thread only: that Shen Yuanhe’s refinement had ended early, and that the family was not saying how.
"That’s enough," Yanning said when her father suggested a fourth. "Any more and it starts looking arranged."

The captured agent’s paired device remained inside the estate. Leon’s suppression around the treasure would soon begin to drift, but the Qiao clan had no second receiver in Moonfall. Once that happened, the reports passing through Redgate Lane would have to carry the deception.
Most of Moonfall heard none of it. That was the point.
The evacuation ran alongside, slowly and on purpose.

Children left with an aunt on a scheduled visit to an allied compound in the second ward. Old account books went out in a crate of ordinary ledgers to a bonded store the family had used for thirty years. Ownership seals and the irreplaceable contracts went three separate directions with three escorts, none of whom knew about the other two. Part of the liquid wealth rode a caravan to Baihe and part rode one going the opposite way.
Yanning’s grandmother refused to move for two hours, then went complaining in a sedan chair beside a guard she had known since he was nine.
Leon walked that traffic all day with his senses open. Containers, axles, harness fittings, the false bottoms of three carts, and the sedan chair all proved clean. He kept looking.
He found it on the fourth wagon out.

Underside of the axle, where a hand could reach in passing while the wagon stood in the loading yard — a mark no bigger than a fingernail, cut into the wood and rubbed with something that made it read as grain. Simpler than a tracker and worse: a marker, the kind that let a watcher confirm a specific vehicle at a distance without following it.
He took it off, put it in a fold, and had the wagon reloaded.
"How long has that been there?" Yanning asked. Her voice had gone flat.
"Days. Maybe since before the raid."

"Then they were mapping our movements before they ever came over the wall." She looked at the yard, at the ordinary busy traffic of her family’s business, and Leon watched her recalculate the entire week. "How much of what I think is normal here is something they arranged?"
"That’s the right question. I don’t have the answer."
Qingyue watched from the gallery above the western yard and said almost nothing.
She came down once, when Shen Baoyuan asked whether the Palace might send someone to look at the estate’s formations.

"No," she said. "Think about what a Jade Moon cultivator standing on your wall tells the man watching you from Redgate Lane. You’d be announcing that this house has a reason to want protection." She turned back toward the stairs. "You have a plan, and it’s a reasonable one. Run it yourselves."
By late afternoon the first real group was ready.

It went out the eastern gate inside an ordinary merchant convoy — eleven wagons of cloth and hardware belonging to three houses, fourteen Shen dependents scattered through it in plain clothes, sitting where families sit. No guards in Shen colors, no escort riding proud at the front. A frightened merchant house quietly moving its people out of the way.
Leon and Yanning watched beneath a concealment screen on the roof of a Shen warehouse as the convoy joined the queue at the gate.
Four hundred paces east, on the flat roof of a dye works, a man in a brown coat had been sitting for most of an hour with a lunch he had not eaten.

He watched the convoy go through. He watched the Shen dependents in it, and the absence of guards, and the way the wagons were loaded for distance. Then he took something small out of his sleeve, held it in his cupped hands for a moment, and put it away.
A thread of qi went west, low and fast, toward Redgate Lane.
"That’s a report," Yanning said.
"That’s a report."
She glanced sideways, and then looked at him properly.
"Why are you smiling?"
"Because he believes us," Leon said.

chapters.title: Chapter 612: A Name This World Will Accept
paragraphs: By the second morning the estate had stopped feeling like a house waiting to be hit.

Masons arrived to repair a section of the eastern wall that had needed repair for four years, and while they worked, two of Yanning’s people seated three new formation nodes into the footing beneath them. A cart of roofing tile came in, and a great deal more than roofing tile came off it. The rear garden gate stayed barred, and the story in the servants’ hall was a spoiled spirit-beast carcass that had to be dealt with.
Shen Yuanhe took Leon down to the cellars before the day started.

"I have moved them," the old man said. "The agent is under the north wing. The Void Immortal stays where he is. Three tokens open the first door, three different ones open the second, and nobody holds a set for both. Not Baoyuan, not Yanning, not me — I hold two of three for each, so I cannot open either alone."
"That’s careful."
"That is a family whose inner estate was breached once already this week." He put a hand on the doorframe. "Show me your seal before you go."
Leon spent an hour on it.

The existing fold had held without Leon standing beside it, but its structure was still formed entirely from his power. That was inadequate for a prison meant to last after he left. He anchored the fold into the chamber’s formations and closed the maintenance loop around the routes between the man’s manifested body and his Ethereal foundation. The estate’s array could now sustain it without Leon.
He walked the old man through it twice, including the parts he disliked.

"It holds against him. It won’t hold against everything," Leon said. "Someone strong from outside who knows what he’s looking at can break it — it’s a wall, not a law. And if he sits with it for months he’ll find the seams. It wants checking."
"Every week," Shen Yuanhe said. "I’ll do it myself."
The registration hall looked exactly as it had the first time: long counters, ink and wax, a queue of caravan clerks arguing about tariff schedules.
The registrar was a different man, older, with a face built for saying no.
Leon set the temporary jade on the counter, cloudy at the edges the way they went as the term ran out.
"Still valid," the registrar said, turning it over. "Renew or convert?"
"Convert," said Shen Yuanhe.
The registrar looked up, looked at the old man properly, and his whole posture changed.
"Elder Shen."
"I am guaranteeing him. Personally."

"Then you know what I have to say next, and I’ll say it anyway because the law requires it." He pulled a heavy ledger over and opened it. "A personal guarantee from a cultivator of your standing means the city holds you responsible. If this man turns out to be a fugitive, an infiltrator, or a criminal under another name, the penalty falls on your seal, your house, and your bond. He goes to a cell. You lose considerably more."
"I helped write half of that law."
"So you did." The registrar dipped his pen. "Then let us be exact about the wording. Vagueness is what ruins guarantors."
It took most of the morning. The registrar rejectedof unknown originas too broad, refused to place the lost realm at an invented location, and would not leave the lineage line blank.
What they finished with was short.

Name: Leon. No recorded surname or lineage.Origin: survivor of a sealed inheritance realm, entrance collapsed; original registration and place of birth unverifiable.Affiliation: none.Guarantor: Shen Yuanhe, personal seal and bond, attesting that the registrant is not a wanted criminal, an infiltrator, or a known agent of a hostile regional power.Prior record: temporary registration, Moonfall eastern gate, transferred and preserved.

"That last line matters," the registrar said without looking up. "Anyone checking sees a stranger who came through a gate and was converted later. A record appearing from nowhere is worse than a thin one."

Leon gave the blood and qi signature into the bowl a second time and shaped what went in exactly as before — stable, coherent, continuous, nothing else. The old man pressed his seal into the wax, laid his cultivation imprint over it, and signed a bond amount that made the registrar’s assistant look up.
The tablet was heavier than the temporary jade, dark green, the city’s mark on one face and no expiry cut into the other.
Outside on the steps, Qingyue read it twice.

"This will do. The Palace will accept it as enough to begin an assessment." She handed it back. "Understand what that sentence contains. It answers whether you may stand at the gate. Nothing past that."

Still more than I had yesterday.Leon turned the tablet over before putting it away. Killing three Void Immortals had not bought him this. Shen Yuanhe’s seal had given him a name this world’s institutions would recognize.
He handled the rest of it that evening, in the guest wing, with the door shut and the lamp out.
The Shen archive material on the Earthmarrow Fern went through first—four generations of feeding records, harvests, recovery notes, and three failed transplant attempts.
"Quarantine’s stable," she said. "It drank about a fifth of what I offered and stopped. I think it’s rationing, which is good — that’s a plant that expects lean years." A pause. "Where are you?"
"Leaving Moonfall in the morning. Going somewhere much harder to hide in."
He told them the shape of it — a major sect, an assessment, elders who would look at him properly for the first time since the crossing.
Seraphine got there first, as usual. "Their guest quarters will have privacy formations."
"They will."
"A formation close enough to keep the world out may also be close enough to listen."
"I know. I’ll take whatever room they give me apart before anyone comes out. If it doesn’t check clean, nobody comes out."
"How long?" Vyra’s voice held an edge. "I have been a passenger since we crossed into this world, Leon. I am not built for it, and neither are my people."
"I can’t give you a date. I can tell you it’s days rather than months."
"That’s not an answer."
"It’s the true one."

Ira cut in, bored-sounding, which was how she sounded when she had decided something was a job. "Leave her be. It’s a placement operation, and you don’t move people into a position until it’s scouted." A beat. "Scout it properly. Rush this and we come out in front of the wrong elder, and we’re all finished."
"Are there gardens?" Loriel asked.
Leon smiled in the dark. "There’ll be gardens."
"Then find out if they have a plant archive. Ask what they keep. Don’t ask about ferns specifically."

Leon sent through four bundles of ordinary clothing purchased in Moonfall. "Wear these when you come out. Keep your signatures down as well. Your energy doesn’t circulate the way theirs does, and that difference may draw attention."
They saw him off at first light.

Shen Baoyuan said very little, which Leon appreciated. He had made his speech already in a garden full of bodies and had the sense not to make it twice. He shook Leon’s hand, said, "The guest wing stays yours," and left it there.

Yanning handed over a folded paper with eleven names on it: factors, an honest ore assayer on the coast road, two innkeepers, and a woman in a port town who could get letters onto Jade Moon supply boats.
"They’ll deal with you on the token," she said. "The ones with a circle beside the name will deal with you without asking questions. The ones without a circle will ask, so give them boring answers."
"Thank you."
"Don’t." She stepped back. "You left us a wall, two prisoners, and a network we can watch. We’re square, and my great-grandfather is going to spend a year telling people otherwise."

Leon put the identity tablet down on the table beside the Shen inner-network token and looked at them together for a moment: a lawful name, and proof that somebody in this world was willing to stand behind it.
Then the light coming through the courtyard changed.

Something silver-green came down out of the morning sky over the estate, long and slender, its underside cut with formation lines that drank the light instead of reflecting it. It made almost no sound at all.
Qingyue stepped off it onto the courtyard stone.
"Bring only what you are willing to have examined," she said.

sentences.text: By the second morning the estate had stopped feeling like a house waiting to be hit.

Masons arrived to repair a section of the eastern wall that had needed repair for four years, and while they worked, two of Yanning’s people seated three new formation nodes into the footing beneath them.
A cart of roofing tile came in, and a great deal more than roofing tile came off it.
The rear garden gate stayed barred, and the story in the servants’ hall was a spoiled spirit-beast carcass that had to be dealt with.
Shen Yuanhe took Leon down to the cellars before the day started.
"I have moved them," the old man said.
"The agent is under the north wing.
The Void Immortal stays where he is.
Three tokens open the first door, three different ones open the second, and nobody holds a set for both.
Not Baoyuan, not Yanning, not me — I hold two of three for each, so I cannot open either alone."
"That’s careful."
"That is a family whose inner estate was breached once already this week." He put a hand on the doorframe.
"Show me your seal before you go."
Leon spent an hour on it.
The existing fold had held without Leon standing beside it, but its structure was still formed entirely from his power.
That was inadequate for a prison meant to last after he left.
He anchored the fold into the chamber’s formations and closed the maintenance loop around the routes between the man’s manifested body and his Ethereal foundation.
The estate’s array could now sustain it without Leon.
He walked the old man through it twice, including the parts he disliked.
"It holds against him.
It won’t hold against everything," Leon said.
"Someone strong from outside who knows what he’s looking at can break it — it’s a wall, not a law.
And if he sits with it for months he’ll find the seams.
It wants checking."
"Every week," Shen Yuanhe said.
"I’ll do it myself."
The registration hall looked exactly as it had the first time: long counters, ink and wax, a queue of caravan clerks arguing about tariff schedules.
The registrar was a different man, older, with a face built for saying no.
Leon set the temporary jade on the counter, cloudy at the edges the way they went as the term ran out.
"Still valid," the registrar said, turning it over.
"Renew or convert?"
"Convert," said Shen Yuanhe.
The registrar looked up, looked at the old man properly, and his whole posture changed.
"Elder Shen."
"I am guaranteeing him.
Personally."
"Then you know what I have to say next, and I’ll say it anyway because the law requires it." He pulled a heavy ledger over and opened it.
"A personal guarantee from a cultivator of your standing means the city holds you responsible.
If this man turns out to be a fugitive, an infiltrator, or a criminal under another name, the penalty falls on your seal, your house, and your bond.
He goes to a cell.
You lose considerably more."
"I helped write half of that law."
"So you did." The registrar dipped his pen.
"Then let us be exact about the wording.
Vagueness is what ruins guarantors."
It took most of the morning.
The registrar rejectedof unknown originas too broad, refused to place the lost realm at an invented location, and would not leave the lineage line blank.
What they finished with was short.
Name: Leon.

No recorded surname or lineage.Origin: survivor of a sealed inheritance realm, entrance collapsed; original registration and place of birth unverifiable.Affiliation: none.Guarantor: Shen Yuanhe, personal seal and bond, attesting that the registrant is not a wanted criminal, an infiltrator, or a known agent of a hostile regional power.Prior record: temporary registration, Moonfall eastern gate, transferred and preserved.
"That last line matters," the registrar said without looking up.
"Anyone checking sees a stranger who came through a gate and was converted later.
A record appearing from nowhere is worse than a thin one."
Leon gave the blood and qi signature into the bowl a second time and shaped what went in exactly as before — stable, coherent, continuous, nothing else.
The old man pressed his seal into the wax, laid his cultivation imprint over it, and signed a bond amount that made the registrar’s assistant look up.
The tablet was heavier than the temporary jade, dark green, the city’s mark on one face and no expiry cut into the other.
Outside on the steps, Qingyue read it twice.
"This will do.
The Palace will accept it as enough to begin an assessment." She handed it back.
"Understand what that sentence contains.
It answers whether you may stand at the gate.
Nothing past that."
Still more than I had yesterday.Leon turned the tablet over before putting it away.
Killing three Void Immortals had not bought him this.
Shen Yuanhe’s seal had given him a name this world’s institutions would recognize.
He handled the rest of it that evening, in the guest wing, with the door shut and the lamp out.
The Shen archive material on the Earthmarrow Fern went through first—four generations of feeding records, harvests, recovery notes, and three failed transplant attempts.
"Quarantine’s stable," she said.
"It drank about a fifth of what I offered and stopped.
I think it’s rationing, which is good — that’s a plant that expects lean years." A pause.
"Where are you?"
"Leaving Moonfall in the morning.
Going somewhere much harder to hide in."
He told them the shape of it — a major sect, an assessment, elders who would look at him properly for the first time since the crossing.
Seraphine got there first, as usual.
"Their guest quarters will have privacy formations."
"They will."
"A formation close enough to keep the world out may also be close enough to listen."
"I know.
I’ll take whatever room they give me apart before anyone comes out.
If it doesn’t check clean, nobody comes out."
"How long?" Vyra’s voice held an edge.
"I have been a passenger since we crossed into this world, Leon.
I am not built for it, and neither are my people."
"I can’t give you a date.
I can tell you it’s days rather than months."
"That’s not an answer."
"It’s the true one."
Ira cut in, bored-sounding, which was how she sounded when she had decided something was a job.
"Leave her be.
It’s a placement operation, and you don’t move people into a position until it’s scouted." A beat.
"Scout it properly.
Rush this and we come out in front of the wrong elder, and we’re all finished."
"Are there gardens?" Loriel asked.
Leon smiled in the dark.
"There’ll be gardens."
"Then find out if they have a plant archive.
Ask what they keep.
Don’t ask about ferns specifically."
Leon sent through four bundles of ordinary clothing purchased in Moonfall.
"Wear these when you come out.
Keep your signatures down as well.
Your energy doesn’t circulate the way theirs does, and that difference may draw attention."
They saw him off at first light.
Shen Baoyuan said very little, which Leon appreciated.
He had made his speech already in a garden full of bodies and had the sense not to make it twice.
He shook Leon’s hand, said, "The guest wing stays yours," and left it there.

Yanning handed over a folded paper with eleven names on it: factors, an honest ore assayer on the coast road, two innkeepers, and a woman in a port town who could get letters onto Jade Moon supply boats.
"They’ll deal with you on the token," she said.
"The ones with a circle beside the name will deal with you without asking questions.
The ones without a circle will ask, so give them boring answers."
"Thank you."
"Don’t." She stepped back.
"You left us a wall, two prisoners, and a network we can watch.
We’re square, and my great-grandfather is going to spend a year telling people otherwise."

Leon put the identity tablet down on the table beside the Shen inner-network token and looked at them together for a moment: a lawful name, and proof that somebody in this world was willing to stand behind it.
Then the light coming through the courtyard changed.
Something silver-green came down out of the morning sky over the estate, long and slender, its underside cut with formation lines that drank the light instead of reflecting it.
It made almost no sound at all.
Qingyue stepped off it onto the courtyard stone.
"Bring only what you are willing to have examined," she said.

chapters.title: Chapter 613: One Night Until Judgment
paragraphs: The vessel was smaller than Leon expected—twelve paces from bow to stern, with a low cabin and an open rear deck. Its pale wooden hull had been grown as one piece rather than joined. Qingyue touched the jade plate in the forward rail, the deck came alive, and Moonfall fell away.
Yanning stood in the courtyard below with one hand raised. Shen Baoyuan had gone inside, since a family being watched does not stand about staring at the sky.
Leon promised nobody he would return soon. The Shens had time, information, stronger walls, and their own competence. A promise made from a sect he had not entered would have meant little.

As the vessel climbed, Moonfall became a shape. Leon saw the wall on its long crooked circuit, mining roads stretching west, and the ore lift over the northern quarter. Beyond them, the Desolation opened into black basins, metal-veined ridges, a vast petrified forest, and a distant grey column where a spiritual storm turned above the south.
He had spent a week learning that city from streets and ledgers. From up here it took eleven seconds to cross.
And that’s one frontier city, on the edge of one region.
"You’re quiet," Qingyue said.
"Recalibrating."
"Good. Most people wait until after they’ve said something foolish."
The journey took the day, and she talked through a fair part of it, which surprised him until he understood she was preparing him.

"Understand what the Palace is before you walk into it," she said. "We’re a sect. Powerful families live inside our territories, but none inherit standing at Jade Moon. Most accepted candidates begin as outer disciples and rise through cultivation, instruction, and service."
"How far up does that go?"

"Outer disciples, inner, core. Then personal disciples, taken by a specific elder and that elder’s responsibility." She adjusted something on the jade plate without looking at it. "Above them elders, above them Supreme Elders, and above all of it the Palace Mistress. That’s as much structure as is useful to you today."
"And your recommendation gets me where?"

"To the reception compound and an examination. That’s all." She glanced over. "Some elders will watch because I brought you personally. Others will assume I found something strange in the Three-Moon Desolation and became sentimental. Tomorrow’s results decide which group was right."
She adjusted the vessel’s course. "I am a Late Earth Immortal. That gives my recommendation weight, but it does not let me rewrite the Palace’s recruitment rules."

Earth Immortal was the local name for an Ethereal Lord, the System’s levels 111 through 130. Qingyue spoke as though Leon had grown up knowing that. He let her continue without revealing that he translated every local realm into a different classification inside his head.
"And unknown origin?"

"Isn’t a disqualification. We take orphans, wanderers, and survivors of collapsed places every year." Her tone flattened. "But if the examination finds a corrupted foundation, a false age, or hostile techniques, they will hold you and determine what you are."
"What’s tomorrow?"

"Three tests, in order." She counted them off. "Bone age — confirms roughly how old you are, and catches crude body possession, age concealment, and reconstructed bodies. Then a cultivation-realm reading, level and stability, built to catch false suppression or a forced advancement. Then the spiritual-root monument."
Leon kept his face still. "Which does what?"

"It reads your elemental structure—how many affinities you possess, how they interact, and what that suggests about your potential." She looked over the rail. "The bone-age test should be routine. The cultivation reading will probably confirm that you’re at least an Archon. I watched you fight the Moonless and the robbers, then examined what you did at the Shen estate. The monument is the part I cannot predict."
That’s the one.

He considered the problem while she talked about the coast. The monument read spiritual roots, meridians, and structures the natives here developed from birth, and he had none of them. It might find affinities without a root, power without local circulation, and a foundation unlike anything it had previously examined.
It might reject him. It might call him abnormal. It might read a great deal more than he wanted read.
He had decided to walk into it regardless, since a year of guessing in frontier markets was the worse outcome. But he built the answer he would need and put it where he could reach it fast.
The realm had its own inheritance. Its methods weren’t the methods out here, and my teachers never explained the mechanism to me — I learned to use it, not to describe it.
It was narrow enough to survive ordinary questioning.
"You’re taking a risk with this," he said, after a while.
"Some."
"Why?"
Qingyue considered it long enough that he thought she might not answer.

"I would rather answer awkward questions for bringing back one unusual candidate than spend the next century wondering whether I abandoned real talent because its origin was inconvenient." She shrugged. "If they turn you away, I’ll be laughed at for a season. I can survive that."
The land changed in the last two hours.

The highlands broke into ridges before giving way to jade-colored water, dark green in the deeps and nearly translucent over the shallows. Islands floated above it. Terraces hung from cliff faces in stacked half-moons, while enormous formation rings on the water drew in the light of a silver moon before sunset.
Somewhere past all of it, in the haze, stood peaks that were not peaks.
The vessel banked south and came down toward a walled compound on a headland — handsome, well kept, and obviously outer.
The reception officials treated Qingyue with immediate respect and Leon with careful neutrality.
Two disciples in pale gray bowed to her the moment she stepped down. An official came out of the hall, bowed lower, and turned to Leon with a face that offered nothing.
"Registration."
Leon handed over the green tablet. The man read it twice and held it to the light to check the seal.
"Shen Yuanhe’s personal bond. Peak Void Immortal, Moonfall." He looked over the top of it. "A significant guarantee for a man with no lineage line."
"He had his reasons."
"He usually does." The official set it down and turned. "Senior Sister?"
She pressed her seal into the wax beside the city’s mark. "My recommendation. He examines tomorrow."

The official entered it in a ledger and read the terms back. Leon received one night in an eastern courtyard and one examination at the first mark after dawn. He had no access to the inner grounds, archives, training terraces, or practice waters. If the examiners found him unsuitable, he would leave that day.
"The courtyard is better than the candidates’ hall," the official added, closing the ledger. "Because Senior Sister Qingyue brought you personally. Nobody here has formed a judgment about you yet."
"Understood."
Qingyue walked him as far as the courtyard gate and no further.

"First mark after dawn. The hall with the double doors on the north side. Don’t be early or late." She turned to go, then stopped. "My name brought you through the gate. It does nothing in that hall tomorrow."
"I’d rather it worked that way."
"Yes," she said. "I thought you might."
The courtyard was small and old and very good: a single-story residence, a walled garden with a stone basin, one gate, and a privacy array laid into the wall in three concentric rings.

Leon activated it and spent forty minutes examining each layer. The residence transmitted no sound or images. The middle ring blocked intrusion, while the outer wards reported attacks, unauthorized departures, and large releases of hostile energy.
Watching for a fight or a runner. Nobody’s listening.
Fair enough. He would have built the same thing.
He left every layer untouched and added a self-contained spatial isolation inside the residence. From outside, the courtyard’s privacy formation continued operating exactly as issued.
He checked it three times, then sat down on the floor in the middle of the room and let the last two weeks arrive all at once.

He carried a lawful identity, Shen Yuanhe’s guarantee, a merchant token, and the knowledge that two prisoners remained safely sealed in Moonfall. Eleven days east, the Qiao clan still believed it had won. In the morning, three tests would decide whether the path ahead remained open.
The courtyard was silent. The garden basin dripped. Out over the water a formation ring hummed to itself as it drank the moonlight.
Leon confirmed the seal one last time, then turned toward the open space in the center of the room.
For the first time since entering the higher world, he finally had a safe place to bring them out.

chapters.title: Chapter 614: The Door Between Worlds
paragraphs: The connection opened, and four people arrived in the middle of a room on the far side of a world.

There was no flare, no tear in the air, and nothing that pressed against the isolation Leon had set inside the residence walls. One moment the floor was empty. The next, Seraphine, Ira, Vyra, and Loriel stood upon it in ordinary Moonfall grey and blue, all four motionless while their bodies adjusted to the pressure of a higher world.
Seraphine moved first.

She crossed the room without a word and caught him by the shoulders. Her hands went immediately to the left one, tracing the place where a chain had torn through it and a spear had later struck the same wound before Leon twisted the weapon away with Space.
"It healed," Leon said.
"I am checking whether it healed properly."
Her thumb moved along the joint and across his collarbone. Then she turned his face toward the lamp and studied his eyes.
"You have lost weight."
"I have been eating noodles."
"That explains it."
Her composure lasted one breath longer. Then she pulled him against her and held on hard enough to make his ribs complain.
"Nearly two weeks," she said into his shoulder.
"Outside," Leon reminded her. Time had passed faster in the dimensional world. The wait had felt longer for them than it had for him.
"That does not improve your position."
"I didn’t think it would."
Ira came up on his other side, inspected his arms, and began counting.
"Two," she said. "More than I expected. Sera, he kept both of them."
"Ira."
"I am being supportive."
She caught the back of Leon’s neck and kissed him without ceremony. The kiss was hard, but the hand that remained at his nape trembled once before becoming still.
"You entered a garden with four Void Immortals," she said quietly. "Alone."
"They weren’t a problem."
"That is the part I hate. You say it as if that makes listening easier."
Vyra had not moved from where she arrived. Her arms were folded, her chin raised, and her posture contained an argument she had been refining since they crossed.
Her gaze travelled over Leon once, lingering on the healed shoulder before returning to his face.
"You survived," she said.
"I said I would."

"You say many things with unreasonable confidence." A fraction of the tension left her shoulders. "Good. I had no desire to explain to my people that I followed a man into another world only for him to die before establishing our position in it."
"Your concern is touching."
"It is practical. Do not make it sentimental." She glanced at Seraphine and Ira, then added, "Keeping us inside was the correct decision. I disliked it. Those statements do not conflict."
That was as close as Vyra came to admitting how carefully she had followed every report.

Loriel had remained a few steps away, watching Seraphine and Ira claim Leon’s attention. When the space around him finally opened, she started forward, hesitated, and then gathered enough courage to cross it.
She wrapped both arms around him.

The embrace was gentler than Seraphine’s and far less confident than Ira’s kiss, but it lasted long enough to make her intention unmistakable. Leon returned it, feeling her relax before she remembered the other women were watching.
Loriel released him quickly, her face turning pink.
"I missed you," she said.
Ira’s smile widened. Loriel saw it and immediately crouched beside the garden door, pressing one palm to the threshold as though that had always been her destination.
"There is water under this building," she announced.
"Is there?" Ira asked innocently.

"It is moving, and it is carrying something. The whole headland sits on a spiritual vein, and someone built the compound directly over it." Loriel kept her attention firmly on the stone. "It is extremely interesting."
"I am sure it suddenly is," Seraphine said.
They gathered around the low table, and Leon explained where they were.

This was only a reception compound outside Jade Moon Palace. Qingyue’s recommendation had bought him one night and one examination. At the first mark after dawn, three artifacts would measure his bone age, cultivation, and spiritual root. The results would decide whether the Palace treated him as a candidate, a curiosity, or a threat.
"If it goes well?" Seraphine asked.
"I gain status and a legitimate place here. Eventually, that gives me room to introduce four attendants I met in a frontier city, supported by real papers and a story that survives questions."
"And if we are discovered tonight?"
"A stranger with an unverifiable history turns out to be hiding four foreigners inside a restricted compound. Nothing I say afterward will matter."
Seraphine disliked the answer, but she accepted it. She still tried once to find a position from which she might remain near the examination hall.
"There is no near," Leon said. "The gate is watched and departures are counted."
"Do not apologize for being correct. It is irritating enough already."
"What do we need to know if the examination goes badly?" Ira asked.

That was useful, so Leon gave her a real answer: the three rings in the courtyard formation, the route between the residence and the north hall, the official controlling the outer ledger, and which of Yanning’s eleven contacts would move people without asking questions. Ira repeated the important parts once and remembered all of them.
Loriel waited until they finished.
"Does the Palace have a medicine court?"
"Certainly."
"A living plant archive?"
"If I am accepted, I will find out what access exists." Leon pointed at her. "I will not ask about ferns."
"I said nothing about ferns."
"Your face did."

They talked long after the practical matters ended. Leon told them about the bones stripped clean in the Desolation, the starving man who had pulled a rusted knife because any stranger approaching him meant danger, and Qingyue cutting the Moonless mark from his shadow. He told them how she had refused to interfere openly in the Shen estate because her presence would have exposed the family, and how Shen Yuanhe had risked his name and fortune to give Leon a lawful identity.
"The merchant’s signature mattered more than the three men you killed," Seraphine said.
"Much more."
Vyra asked about Qingyue.

"She is a Late Earth Immortal," Leon said. "Three named realms above me, with two complete realms between us. She is disciplined, direct, and willing to risk her standing rather than leave something important in a frontier city."
"I want to dislike her," Vyra said.

"Noted."
"Good. I’m not saying it twice."
They talked briefly about the morning, the way people talk in the dark when nobody wants to properly start the day.
"Three tests," Ira said. "Which one worries you?"
"The third."
"Then don’t think about it until it’s in front of you. You’ll only rehearse yourself into looking rehearsed."

"We know," Seraphine said. Then, more quietly: "Leon. Whatever they measure in there — it won’t be all of you. Remember that when they say a number."

The examination hall was smaller than expected: bare grey stone, a high ceiling, and three artifacts beneath shafts of morning light. Qingyue stood beside a lean elder in dark blue and four junior officials.
Her eyes passed over Leon’s calmer expression, but she asked nothing.
The elder rested one hand upon a pale stone ring.
"Age first," he said. "If the record lies, nothing after it matters."

chapters.title: Chapter 617: Only Golden Core
paragraphs: The pale ring was warm.

Leon placed his hand where the examiner indicated and felt the artifact sweep through bone, marrow, and the bond between body and soul. He held his foundation still and allowed it to see what it had been made to measure.
Age. Integration. Possession. Reconstruction.
It passed over his second heart without understanding it. The dimensional world remained deeper still, untouched by the ring’s awareness.
Three lines appeared upon the stone.
Bone Age: Twenty-Two Years
Body–Soul Integration: Unbroken
No Possession, Reconstruction, or Age Concealment Detected
One junior official inhaled sharply.
Elder Wen turned his head. "Twenty-two?"
"Yes, Elder."
"Again."
The second reading took longer. It reached through Leon by another route and returned the same three lines.

Elder Wen studied Leon rather than the artifact this time. Leon understood why. Twenty-two-year-olds were not supposed to possess his stillness, his reflexes, or the habit of watching every door in a room.
"Your bearing is older than your bones," Wen said.
"The place where I grew up did not leave much room to be young."
Qingyue had expected him to be young by cultivator standards. Perhaps forty. Even that would have made his apparent strength extraordinary. Twenty-two changed the scale of the problem.
Elder Wen gestured toward the next artifact.
"Cultivation."

The second instrument was a shallow basin of dark metal filled with something that resembled neither water nor light. Leon placed both hands into it. The substance climbed his forearms without wetting them.
It began at the lowest cultivation realm and tested upward. Halfway through, the formation hesitated. Its light faded, returned, and began the entire sequence again.
One junior frowned at his plate. "Elder—"
"I see it. Do not interfere."
The reading slowed at the same place. Then the dark surface steadied and characters formed above it.
Realm: Peak Golden Core
Leon translated the result privately.
Level 50. Peak Ascendant.
Behind him, Qingyue made a very small sound.
It was the loudest thing in the hall.

He turned. Her composure had cracked by less than a finger’s width, but Leon had spent four days travelling through the Desolation with her and several more in Moonfall. He had never seen her openly surprised.
No one else in the hall understood why. A twenty-two-year-old at Peak Golden Core was highly talented, but the result alone did not justify disbelief.
Qingyue knew what the basin did not show.

She had found Leon holding his ground against the Moonless Shadow Leopard in the Desolation, an Earth Immortal beast that could have killed most Void Immortals within seconds. On the road, he had then killed seven Dao Palace cultivators and their Early-stage Void Immortal leader. Later, in the Shen estate, he had killed three Void Immortals and captured a fourth with his immortal foundation sealed.
Qingyue had explained those feats by assuming Leon’s true cultivation was concealed—Dao Palace, perhaps, with techniques refined enough to make him look weaker than he was.
Peak Golden Core stripped that explanation away.
She had not overestimated him. She had underestimated him by an absurd margin.
Her expression settled before any of the officials could read more from it, and she said nothing. They did not know his combat record, and she had no intention of revealing it without his permission.
Elder Wen was studying the basin rather than Qingyue. The formation had hesitated and restarted before producing its answer, which was reason enough for him to distrust a routine reading.
"Drain it. Reseat it. Secondary formation and full calibration."

Two officials lifted the dark basin while the others opened the plinth and inspected every formation node. Elder Wen laid a second array beneath it to detect suppression, borrowed power, false advancement, and anything that might deliberately lower the result.
Leon submitted to the examination without comment.
Twenty minutes later, the same words appeared.
Realm: Peak Golden Core

The officials checked the suppression formation first. Its twelve nodes remained clear. A borrowed technique would have left a second rhythm in the basin; none appeared. A damaged breakthrough would have produced fractures or turbulence; Leon’s reading remained smooth enough to irritate Elder Wen further.
At the examiner’s order, one junior brought a reference crystal used for testing the basin itself. It displayed exactly the value carved into its base.
No one could blame the instrument anymore.
Elder Wen kept one hand in the dark fluid as he studied the internal flow.

"The artifact is functioning," he said. "There is no false suppression, forced advancement, corrupted foundation, parasitic technique, or borrowed cultivation. His realm is real. Everything surrounding the realm is the anomaly."
"Explain," Qingyue said.
Wen lifted one finger.
"His energy density is comparable to that of a strong Dao Palace cultivator. I mean density, not combat output. What he possesses is compressed far beyond the normal limit of Golden Core."
A second finger rose.
"His foundation is more complete than the realm requires. There are Dao Palace cultivators inside this Palace with less stable foundations."
Then a third.
"His body, spirit, and power support one another without a weak seam. That is rare at any realm. At twenty-two, I would have called it impossible yesterday."
Wen lowered his hand and frowned at Leon’s submerged arms.
"I cannot tell you how he accomplished it. His energy does not circulate along any meridian structure I recognize. I have examined cultivators for two centuries, and I cannot map his channels."
The four junior officials stared openly now.
"Where did you cultivate?" Wen asked.
Leon gave the answer he had prepared during the vessel journey.

"Inside a sealed inheritance realm. I do not know who created it. Its methods were different from the ones used here. I have been outside long enough to buy a children’s primer on meridians, and I understood only half of it." He allowed some genuine frustration into his voice. "I was taught how to use what I possess. Nobody explained why it worked. When the entrance collapsed, I emerged with no teacher and no way back."
"That is an unsatisfying answer."
"It is the answer I have. If I invented something better, people here would expose it within a week."
Elder Wen regarded him for several breaths, then grunted.
"That last sentence is the most convincing part."

For Qingyue, the missing history finally began to make sense. A twenty-two-year-old with this foundation could not have developed openly. Any clan that found him as a child would have built its future around him, while any sect would have recorded every breakthrough. If Leon had grown anywhere connected to ordinary civilization, someone would already have claimed him.
His lack of history was no longer the greatest weakness in his story. It was evidence supporting it.
Elder Wen turned to the recording official.
"Two separate entries. Realm: Peak Golden Core. Then: energy density and foundation quality comparable to Dao Palace; upper limit undetermined. Do not combine them."
The official wrote each line carefully.
Wen looked toward the final artifact.

It was a monument rather than an instrument—a dark stone slab nearly three meters high, worn smooth around its base. Nine faint channels ran across its face, surrounded by characters in a script Leon had not seen anywhere in Moonfall.
"Remove the routine candidate calibration," Wen ordered. "Use the old setting."
One junior hesitated. "Elder, that setting has not been used in—"

"I know when it was last used. This morning has given us a twenty-two-year-old Peak Golden Core cultivator with Dao Palace-level energy density and a foundation I cannot map. I will not trust a routine reading."
The officials spent ten minutes waking the older formations. Something deep inside the monument stirred with a sound like a bell struck beneath water.
Qingyue moved to Leon’s side. She had expected to defend an unusual recommendation. Now she suspected the first two tests had been the ordinary part.
"Place your palm flat," Wen said. "Do not push power into it. The monument will take what it needs."
Leon touched the cold stone.
Nothing happened.
Then the first dormant channel opened and burned red.
Elder Wen leaned forward.
"Fire," he whispered.

chapters.title: Chapter 618: The Monument’s Ninth Answer
paragraphs: Red light climbed the first channel and remained at its peak, steady as a lamp.
The recording official lifted his brush.
"One elemental compatibility. Fire—"
The second channel opened.
Blue flowed upward through the stone. When it met the red at the top, neither light weakened.
The official stopped writing.
"Water," Elder Wen said.

The third compatibility rose more slowly. Amber gathered from the base and settled into its channel with a weight Leon could feel beneath his palm. Pale green followed, always moving, the light refusing to remain still anywhere inside its path.
Four elements in less than a minute.
"A four-element spiritual root," one junior said. "Elder, that is—"
"Exceptional," Wen finished. "You may stop counting aloud."
The fifth channel ignored him.
Lightning branched upward in violet-white forks, separating and reforming faster than the eye could follow. The sixth filled with silver-blue frost that spread from the base in crystalline fans.
Wen stopped naming the results.
Lightning and ice burned beside each other without conflict. He had once read an entire study written from nine recorded cases of that pairing. Leon had six elements, and the monument had not slowed.
The seventh channel filled with gold.

The eighth did not seem to fill at all. A black-violet depth opened inside the stone, extending inward rather than rising. It gave off no light, yet everyone in the room could see it. Darkness settled one hand’s width from Light, and neither devoured the other.
Elder Wen stepped backward.
"Light and Darkness," he said. "Together."
One junior put down his brush. Pretending this remained an ordinary examination had become impossible.
Leon kept his palm flat and his expression calm.
His spatial perception had entered the monument with its power. He could feel the formations below, the ancient current moving through the base, and the architecture of the artifact itself.
Nine channels.
Exactly nine.

Eight already held a result, and the monument had brushed against other parts of Leon’s foundation without possessing anywhere to place them. It was not concealing what it found. It simply had no language or structure for anything beyond the sockets its maker had carved.
The ninth channel opened.
Space did not burn, flow, or crystallize. The monument’s outline stopped agreeing with itself. Along the final channel, the wall behind the stone appeared in two places at once.
Then the artifact stopped searching.
Leon felt its attention retract and settle. It had filled every channel it possessed and concluded its task.
This is the monument’s limit. Not mine.
There was no need for anyone else to learn that.
He buried the realization and kept his breathing unchanged.
The nine lights turned inward.

Fire and Water met first without extinguishing each other. Earth rose beneath them and held. Wind threaded through all three. Lightning branched through the structure while Ice formed around it without shattering. Light and Darkness approached last, remaining whole and separate even when Space folded around them.
The combined phenomenon emerged above the monument.
Nine colors turned inside a single sphere, every affinity distinct yet perfectly balanced with the rest.
Ancient golden characters appeared across the stone.
Elder Wen read them once in silence. When he tried aloud, his voice failed and he had to begin again.
"Ninefold Elemental Harmony Spiritual Root."
Nobody answered him.
A bell rang somewhere above the reception compound.
The sound travelled through the stone as strongly as it travelled through the air. A second bell answered before the first echo faded. Then a third.
The junior officials went pale as they counted.
Four.
Five.
Six.
Qingyue turned toward the ceiling, her lips parted.
Seven.
Eight.
Nine.

The merged light passed through the hall’s roof without damaging it and rose into the clear morning sky. Nine colors braided together in a pillar visible from every terrace, courtyard, and practice ground around the reception compound.
Elder Wen stared at the golden classification.
"More than three thousand years," he said. "The last confirmed bearer appeared over three thousand years ago. He eventually became a Heaven Immortal."
Several officials looked at Leon as if the final realm had already been promised.
Wen noticed.

"The spiritual root did not hand that man his cultivation," he said sharply. "It gave him compatibility. He still spent centuries surviving, learning, and breaking through. Record the result without inventing a destiny around it."
"What became of his lineage?" one junior asked before remembering this was not a lecture.

Wen’s eyes remained on the monument. "It ended. His descendants inherited fragments—two elements in one generation, three in another, never the harmony itself. The Palace retained his records, but no complete method could be passed to someone who did not share his constitution."
That answer changed the mood again. Leon was not merely repeating a known inheritance. If accepted, the Palace would need to build a path around him from surviving pieces.
The official picked up his brush, though his hand was no longer steady.
Leon removed his palm.
The lights did not fade. All nine channels remained saturated, their colors moving slowly beneath the dark surface.
Wen inspected the base and sent a thread of qi through its release formation.
"Nothing is broken," he said after a moment. "The monument took in more than it can release quickly. Four days, perhaps six, before it can examine anyone else."
The first elders arrived before the fourth minute ended.
They entered quickly and with visible irritation, clearly expecting an artifact failure. One was halfway through demanding an explanation when he saw the monument.
He stopped.

The others saw the same sequence: a young man in plain Moonfall clothing; a record showing a bone age of twenty-two; Peak Golden Core cultivation; a separate note describing Dao Palace-level density and foundation quality; nine saturated channels; and a forgotten classification burning in gold.
More elders arrived. Then more after them.

The nine bells had not identified a candidate or even confirmed that the event came from an examination. They had only announced that an ancient threshold had been reached. That uncertainty drew senior cultivators faster than a detailed message would have. Each new arrival entered prepared for several possibilities and abandoned all of them after seeing Leon.

One elder asked whether the light could have been produced by nine candidates touching the stone together. Elder Wen pointed silently at the single handprint still glowing at its center. The elder did not ask a second question.

Elder Wen tried three times to restore order. He abandoned the effort when the eleventh arrival began arguing about the monument’s calibration history while another elder sent a message token out of the hall.
"All records remain on this table," Wen snapped. "No copies leave until the Palace decides how this result will be handled."
Qingyue stayed beside Leon.

She had entered the hall prepared to endure a season of ridicule if her recommendation proved foolish. That concern had died somewhere around the eighth element. She had not yet decided what had replaced it.
An old elder in green was the first to stop staring at the artifact and examine Leon himself.
"Whose personal disciple is he?" the man asked.
"No one’s," Qingyue said.
Every elder in the room looked at Leon again.
This time, they were not examining him.
They were calculating.

The recording official lifted his brush.
"One elemental compatibility.

The second channel opened.
Blue flowed upward through the stone.

Space did not burn, flow, or crystallize.

Six.

Seven.
Eight.

chapters.title: Chapter 619: Whose Disciple Is He?
paragraphs: The elder in green reacted first.

"Then this is still a recruitment matter." He stepped forward before anyone could object. "Young friend, I hold the Verdant Tide inheritance, the only lineage in Jade Moon Palace that has successfully trained a triple-element constitution. Become my personal disciple. You will receive core status immediately and a private cultivation ground upon the third terrace."
"You intend to teach nine elements with a water-and-wood inheritance?" a woman behind him asked.
"I intend to teach him two foundations properly instead of drowning him in nine at once. That is already more responsible than whatever you are about to offer."
She ignored him and addressed Leon.

"I hold the Frostmoon sword lineage. Ice and Lightning appeared in adjacent channels without degrading each other. I offer personal instruction, immediate core status, and access to the sword vault beneath the second peak."
An elder wearing a formation master’s sash cut in.
"His Space affinity alone makes sword instruction a waste. The deep formation halls have three incomplete spatial arrays left by former Palace Mistresses. I will open all three to him."
"So he can spend fifty years repairing your failures?"
"So he can learn from work none of you are qualified to understand."
Order disappeared after that.

Leon listened without committing to anyone. He asked what a private cultivation ground provided, whether an inheritance could be studied without formally accepting its lineage, and how many personal disciples the Verdant Tide elder already taught.
The last question produced a pause.
"Seven," the elder admitted.
"Nine," the Frostmoon elder corrected. "He forgot the two in seclusion."
"They require no daily instruction."
"Neither, apparently, do the seven who remain visible."
Ira would have enjoyed the room.

The offers grew with every interruption. Monthly allotments were named that made the junior officials exchange looks. One elder promised access to restricted medicines. Leon paid more attention to that than he showed. Another offered a residence near the inner practice lake, while a third guaranteed him a position above ordinary core disciples from the moment he entered.

An elderly woman from the medicine court offered something different: no fixed inheritance at all. She would assemble nine instructors under one schedule and use the court’s resources to monitor conflict between his affinities. For Leon, unrestricted medicine-court access also meant Loriel—once he could introduce her safely—would eventually have a place to ask questions that no one in the hall yet knew existed.
Leon nearly asked for the details before noticing three other elders react as though she had proposed dividing Palace territory.
That offer is politically expensive,he realized.Which means she either wants the result badly or believes everyone else will fail him.
Each offer taught Leon something.

Nobody described Jade Moon Palace as a whole. They described the part they controlled—their peak, vault, medicine hall, inheritance, or cultivation ground—and presented it as the center of the sect. Accepting any one of them would provide a powerful protector while tying him to that protector’s rivals.

The competition was useful, but it also revealed the danger of choosing too quickly. A generous monthly allotment could be revised. Permission to enter a vault could become leverage. A personal disciple inherited not only a teacher’s knowledge, but also that teacher’s obligations, grudges, and unfinished disputes.
Leon knew too little about any of them to distinguish a powerful mentor from a comfortable trap.
Elder Wen stood beside the recording table with both hands flat upon it.
"The candidate has not been formally admitted," he said for the third time.
Nobody listened.
"The examination is not complete until I sign it."
An elder leaned over, took the brush, and placed it in his hand.
"Then sign faster."
The Supreme Elders arrived before Wen could decide whether throwing the brush would damage his dignity.
Four entered, and the hall rearranged itself around them without a command. Ordinary elders stepped aside. Offers became more measured, though no less ambitious.
The final Supreme Elder was a tall woman in white and pale green. Her hair was pinned severely, and her expression suggested she had crossed a considerable distance to be irritated in person.
Qingyue straightened.
Her master,Leon realized.

The woman did not speak to Qingyue first. She inspected the monument, read the golden characters, and checked the saturated channels. At the recording table, she reviewed the bone-age result, the cultivation result, and the separate foundation note.
Then she questioned Elder Wen.
"Was the cultivation basin reseated?"
"Completely."
"Was the secondary formation laid before or after the anomalous reading?"
"After the first. The second result was identical."
"Any suppression, corruption, borrowed power, or forced advancement?"
"None."
"Was the old calibration active before he touched the monument?"
"Yes, Supreme Elder."
She inclined her head. "Then the record stands."
Only then did she turn to Qingyue.
"You brought him."
"I did, Master."
"From where?"

"The Western Starfall Marches. I found him in the Desolation with a Moonless hunting him. He had no sect, clan, or permanent registration, and his explanation was incomplete. I observed his conduct over several days, verified what I could, and chose to bring him for examination rather than leave the decision to a delayed report."
The Supreme Elder regarded her disciple for a moment.
"You were correct to notice him, correct to verify him, and correct to bring him yourself. Most disciples of your standing would have done one of those things and considered themselves diligent."
The hall, which had been loudly discussing Leon’s future, became interested in Qingyue instead.
Qingyue bowed with calm dignity.
"Thank you, Master."
Entirely deliberate,she assured herself.Every part of it.

She refused to think about how close she had come to walking past Leon on the ridge, or the explanations she had prepared during the flight in case the Palace found nothing exceptional. She had recognized that he deserved examination. That part was true, and she accepted the praise for it.
Her master faced Leon.

"I hold the Silent Tide inheritance. I will not claim it was designed for nine elements. Nothing in this Palace was. Anyone who has told you otherwise this morning is selling you something." Her eyes moved briefly across the gathered elders. "I have accepted four personal disciples in three hundred years. All four are alive. Not everyone here can say the same."
Several elders looked offended. None contradicted her.
"I offer you personal discipleship," she continued. "One teacher, not nine competing inheritances, and enough authority to obtain specialists when you require them."
It was the most sensible offer Leon had heard.
It still settled nothing.

Two other Supreme Elders invoked their own claims immediately. One controlled the Palace’s oldest elemental archive. Another had personally guided three disciples to the Heaven Immortal threshold and saw no reason to yield to an inheritance better suited to concealment than harmony.

The argument remained verbal. Nobody released cultivation pressure or reached for a weapon. Even so, four Supreme Elders and a dozen elders speaking across one another filled the hall more completely than a battle cry.
Elder Wen stopped pretending the examination still belonged to him.
Then the noise ended.
It did not fade. It vanished across two heartbeats, starting near the monument and spreading through the room.
Every Supreme Elder turned toward the same place.
A veiled woman stood beside the nine-colored stone.
No door had opened.
Leon had not felt her arrive.
