chapters.title: Chapter 620: The Master Above Them All
paragraphs: Leon’s spatial perception had covered the entire hall since the first elders arrived.
It had noticed message tokens, hidden formation threads, and every person who crossed the doors. The woman beside the monument had passed through all of it without creating a single disturbance.
That was more alarming than any display of pressure.

She wore pale green and silver-grey robes without ornament. A silver veil covered the lower half of her face. What little Leon could see above it made the veil feel like a decision rather than decoration.
Every elder bowed.
The Supreme Elders bowed lower.
"Palace Mistress," Qingyue’s master said.
Leon bowed with the rest and examined the newcomer only as far as courtesy allowed.

Qingyue was a Late Earth Immortal. The Palace Mistress stood only one named realm above her, but the distance between them was enormous. Leon recognized the completed density and self-contained power of a Peak Heaven Immortal.
Peak Ethereal Sovereign,he translated privately.
She was the strongest publicly active cultivator in Jade Moon Palace.
The Palace Mistress looked first at the saturated monument, then at the examination record. She read every entry without asking another person to summarize it.
"Twenty-two," she said. "Peak Golden Core. Dao Palace-level density and a foundation the examiner cannot map. Nine affinities held in complete balance."
Her gaze settled upon Leon.
There was no invasive pressure in it. She simply watched him with the patience of someone accustomed to discovering more than people intended to show.
"Your foundation is stranger than the monument’s classification explains," she said. "I will not attempt to explain it in a hall containing thirty witnesses."
"I would prefer that," Leon replied.
"I expected you would."
She turned toward the assembled elders.
"The recruitment argument is over."
Nobody protested.

"I offer Leon direct discipleship. Not outer discipleship, inner discipleship, or core status awaiting further consideration. If he accepts, he will receive instruction and protection appropriate to his standing from the day he enters."

Several elders concealed disappointment badly. The Frostmoon elder glanced at the monument as if searching for one final argument, while the Verdant Tide elder appeared to calculate whether speaking would damage him more than silence.
The Palace Mistress continued before either could decide.

"His constitution will be studied with his knowledge and cooperation. He is a disciple of Jade Moon Palace, not an artifact the Palace has acquired. His resources and access will be determined after someone asks what he needs, which none of you managed to do before offering him your vaults."
The formation elder looked away.
Then the Palace Mistress addressed Leon again.
"That is my offer. You may refuse it. Before you answer, tell me what you came here seeking."
The question was more useful than every promise he had heard that morning.

"A place in this world that cannot be erased by the first powerful person who dislikes my origin," Leon said. "Knowledge of its cultivation, history, and powers. A road upward that does not require me to pretend I understand traditions I encountered less than two weeks ago."
"And loyalty?"
"Earned in both directions."
The hall became very still.
One Supreme Elder frowned at the answer. The Palace Mistress did not.

"Good," she said. "Promises given too quickly are worth very little. I offer protection, instruction, and the standing of my direct disciple. In return, you will obey the Palace’s rules while you live within it, protect its disciples when doing so does not demand the sacrifice of everything you are responsible for, and speak honestly when you do not understand what is being asked of you."
No demand to expose the dimensional world. No oath to surrender the people within it. No claim over every technique he possessed.
Leon considered the offer for four seconds, three more than he required.

The Palace Mistress was the strongest person he had encountered in this world. Standing beneath her authority ended the competition immediately. One direct relationship was safer than owing pieces of himself to eleven elders with competing peaks and inheritances.
More importantly, she had recognized that his cooperation mattered before asking for it.
Leon bowed in the formal manner Yanning had taught him during their journey toward Moonfall, roughly ten days earlier. Neither of them had imagined where he would first use it.
"Then I accept," he said. "Master."
Something shifted at the edge of the Palace Mistress’s veil. It might have been the beginning of a smile.

She lifted one hand. A silver-green thread of light crossed the space between them and settled around Leon’s identity tablet inside his sleeve. It did not overwrite Shen Yuanhe’s guarantee. It added a second imprint above it: the personal mark of Jade Moon Palace’s ruler.
"Your admission is complete," she said.
Elder Wen looked at the unsigned examination record, then silently signed it.
Qingyue’s master was the first Supreme Elder to bow toward Leon in acknowledgement of the new relationship.
"Junior Uncle," she said.
The title travelled through the hall like a second, much quieter phenomenon.
Leon looked at the woman who had lived for centuries and taught Qingyue, then at the ordinary elders realizing what the Palace Mistress’s direct discipleship did to seniority.
The Palace Mistress spared him from answering immediately.
"Formal modes of address can wait until he has learned why half of them are absurd," she said.
Qingyue lowered her gaze, but Leon saw the corner of her mouth move. A few ordinary elders appeared personally wounded by the ruling.
The Palace Mistress faced the room.

"This morning’s exact record is sealed. His bone age, realm, foundation anomaly, nine affinities, and the classification shown by the monument will not leave the Palace through any channel I have not authorized. That instruction includes the officials who recorded it and every elder who entered afterward."
One elder glanced toward the ceiling.
"Palace Mistress, the bells—"

"Nine bells rang, and half the reception compound saw a nine-colored pillar. We will not pretend otherwise. Nor will we erase memories or confine witnesses. A sect that visibly buries a discovery merely invites outsiders to dig."
Her voice remained quiet, but nobody missed a word.

"Let the rumor say Jade Moon Palace found an exceptional disciple. Rumor requires no assistance beyond that. It will not carry his name, age, cultivation, elements, or spiritual-root classification from anyone in this room."
The disappointed elders bowed their acceptance one by one.

The Palace Mistress assigned Qingyue’s master to oversee the sealing of the original record and ordered Elder Wen to prepare a second, public entry containing only Leon’s lawful admission and the fact that his aptitude met the Palace’s highest recruitment standard. The two records would agree without giving an outsider the useful details.
"Do not invent a lesser result," she said. "A false record creates contradictions. Omission is sufficient."
Elder Wen nodded, visibly relieved to receive an instruction that belonged in an examination hall.

Qingyue remained beside her master, looking calmer than she had any right to feel. Elder Wen began collecting the record slates himself. The four junior officials moved with the stiff care of people who had started the morning expecting ordinary paperwork and ended it under a direct order from the Palace Mistress.

Outside, the nine-colored pillar had already begun to fade. Across the terraces, hundreds of disciples would be inventing explanations. By sunset, every major power near the jade sea would know that the Palace bells had rung nine times.
They would not know for whom.
The Palace Mistress stepped away from the monument and gestured toward the inner doors.
"Come, disciple. You have been offered a dozen inheritances by people who know almost nothing about you. We will begin by correcting that."
Leon followed.
Behind him, the Ninefold Elemental Harmony monument continued to burn with all nine colors, filled to the limit of what its makers had imagined.
It had named nine parts of him.
For now, nine were enough.

She read every entry without asking another person to summarize it.
"Twenty-two," she said.
"Peak Golden Core.
Dao Palace-level density and a foundation the examiner cannot map.
Nine affinities held in complete balance."
Her gaze settled upon Leon.
There was no invasive pressure in it.
She simply watched him with the patience of someone accustomed to discovering more than people intended to show.
"Your foundation is stranger than the monument’s classification explains," she said.
"I will not attempt to explain it in a hall containing thirty witnesses."
"I would prefer that," Leon replied.
"I expected you would."
She turned toward the assembled elders.
"The recruitment argument is over."
Nobody protested.
"I offer Leon direct discipleship.
Not outer discipleship, inner discipleship, or core status awaiting further consideration.
If he accepts, he will receive instruction and protection appropriate to his standing from the day he enters."
Several elders concealed disappointment badly.
The Frostmoon elder glanced at the monument as if searching for one final argument, while the Verdant Tide elder appeared to calculate whether speaking would damage him more than silence.
The Palace Mistress continued before either could decide.
"His constitution will be studied with his knowledge and cooperation.
He is a disciple of Jade Moon Palace, not an artifact the Palace has acquired.
His resources and access will be determined after someone asks what he needs, which none of you managed to do before offering him your vaults."
The formation elder looked away.
Then the Palace Mistress addressed Leon again.
"That is my offer.
You may refuse it.
Before you answer, tell me what you came here seeking."
The question was more useful than every promise he had heard that morning.
"A place in this world that cannot be erased by the first powerful person who dislikes my origin," Leon said.
"Knowledge of its cultivation, history, and powers.
A road upward that does not require me to pretend I understand traditions I encountered less than two weeks ago."
"And loyalty?"
"Earned in both directions."
The hall became very still.
One Supreme Elder frowned at the answer.
The Palace Mistress did not.
"Good," she said.
"Promises given too quickly are worth very little.
I offer protection, instruction, and the standing of my direct disciple.

In return, you will obey the Palace’s rules while you live within it, protect its disciples when doing so does not demand the sacrifice of everything you are responsible for, and speak honestly when you do not understand what is being asked of you."
No demand to expose the dimensional world.
No oath to surrender the people within it.
No claim over every technique he possessed.
Leon considered the offer for four seconds, three more than he required.
The Palace Mistress was the strongest person he had encountered in this world.
Standing beneath her authority ended the competition immediately.
One direct relationship was safer than owing pieces of himself to eleven elders with competing peaks and inheritances.
More importantly, she had recognized that his cooperation mattered before asking for it.
Leon bowed in the formal manner Yanning had taught him during their journey toward Moonfall, roughly ten days earlier.
Neither of them had imagined where he would first use it.
"Then I accept," he said.
"Master."
Something shifted at the edge of the Palace Mistress’s veil.
It might have been the beginning of a smile.
She lifted one hand.
A silver-green thread of light crossed the space between them and settled around Leon’s identity tablet inside his sleeve.
It did not overwrite Shen Yuanhe’s guarantee.
It added a second imprint above it: the personal mark of Jade Moon Palace’s ruler.
"Your admission is complete," she said.
Elder Wen looked at the unsigned examination record, then silently signed it.
Qingyue’s master was the first Supreme Elder to bow toward Leon in acknowledgement of the new relationship.
"Junior Uncle," she said.
The title travelled through the hall like a second, much quieter phenomenon.
Leon looked at the woman who had lived for centuries and taught Qingyue, then at the ordinary elders realizing what the Palace Mistress’s direct discipleship did to seniority.
The Palace Mistress spared him from answering immediately.
"Formal modes of address can wait until he has learned why half of them are absurd," she said.
Qingyue lowered her gaze, but Leon saw the corner of her mouth move.
A few ordinary elders appeared personally wounded by the ruling.
The Palace Mistress faced the room.
"This morning’s exact record is sealed.
His bone age, realm, foundation anomaly, nine affinities, and the classification shown by the monument will not leave the Palace through any channel I have not authorized.
That instruction includes the officials who recorded it and every elder who entered afterward."
One elder glanced toward the ceiling.
"Palace Mistress, the bells—"
"Nine bells rang, and half the reception compound saw a nine-colored pillar.
We will not pretend otherwise.
Nor will we erase memories or confine witnesses.
A sect that visibly buries a discovery merely invites outsiders to dig."
Her voice remained quiet, but nobody missed a word.
"Let the rumor say Jade Moon Palace found an exceptional disciple.
Rumor requires no assistance beyond that.
It will not carry his name, age, cultivation, elements, or spiritual-root classification from anyone in this room."
The disappointed elders bowed their acceptance one by one.

The Palace Mistress assigned Qingyue’s master to oversee the sealing of the original record and ordered Elder Wen to prepare a second, public entry containing only Leon’s lawful admission and the fact that his aptitude met the Palace’s highest recruitment standard.
The two records would agree without giving an outsider the useful details.
"Do not invent a lesser result," she said.
"A false record creates contradictions.
Omission is sufficient."
Elder Wen nodded, visibly relieved to receive an instruction that belonged in an examination hall.
Qingyue remained beside her master, looking calmer than she had any right to feel.
Elder Wen began collecting the record slates himself.
The four junior officials moved with the stiff care of people who had started the morning expecting ordinary paperwork and ended it under a direct order from the Palace Mistress.
Outside, the nine-colored pillar had already begun to fade.
Across the terraces, hundreds of disciples would be inventing explanations.
By sunset, every major power near the jade sea would know that the Palace bells had rung nine times.
They would not know for whom.
The Palace Mistress stepped away from the monument and gestured toward the inner doors.
"Come, disciple.
You have been offered a dozen inheritances by people who know almost nothing about you.
We will begin by correcting that."
Leon followed.
Behind him, the Ninefold Elemental Harmony monument continued to burn with all nine colors, filled to the limit of what its makers had imagined.
It had named nine parts of him.
For now, nine were enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 621: The Truth He Could Afford
paragraphs: The inner doors closed behind them and the noise of the examination compound stopped as though it had been switched off.

Ji Liansu did not hurry. She walked ahead of Leon along a corridor of pale stone that opened, after perhaps two hundred paces, onto a terrace on the seaward face of the peak — and then into a chamber that surprised him by being ordinary.

He had expected jade and gold. What he found was a plain room with a low table, four cushions, and a shallow channel of water running across the floor from one wall to the other, six inches wide, carrying a slow current out through a gap in the stone and down the cliff face. The only decoration was the water. Everything else had been left alone.
She sat, indicated the cushion across from her, and touched two fingers to the table.
The formations closed. Leon felt them go up in layers, and then felt something else settle over the room — a quieter, older working that had nothing to do with keeping people out.
"Nothing said in this room is recorded," Ji Liansu said. "I will not repeat any of it unless the Palace’s survival requires me to. My name is Ji Liansu. You may use it here. Outside, you will not."
"Understood."
"Good." She folded her hands. "Then I will ask the question I did not ask in the hall, in front of thirty people who would have written down your answer."
Leon waited.

"The monument named nine," she said. "I have read the record twice and I have looked at you once, which was sufficient. Your foundation contains more than that classification accounts for." Her eyes did not move from his face. "Why did it stop?"
There it is.

He had known this was coming since the moment she saidI would rather understand it than announce itin front of the assembled elders. He had spent the walk here deciding what he could afford, and he had arrived at an answer he did not entirely like and could not improve.

The woman across the table was a Peak Heaven Immortal. He had no idea what that meant in practical terms and no intention of finding out. In a direct confrontation, he had no realistic way to resist her for even a second. But she had stood in a hall full of elders bidding for him and saidwith his cooperation, andnobody has troubled to ask him what he needs. She had offered him room to choose when nobody present could have forced her to.
A complete lie now would be discovered eventually. And when it was, everything after it would be poisoned.
"It stopped because it ran out of channels," Leon said.
Ji Liansu’s expression did not change.

"Nine sockets cut into the stone," he went on. "I could feel it working. It was honest — it took what I had and pushed each piece into the nearest place it understood. When the ninth filled, it had nowhere left to ask a question, so it stopped asking." He met her eyes. "That was the monument’s limit. Not mine."
"What else is in you?"
"That’s the part I’m not going to answer."
"No," she agreed. "I did not expect you to. What else?"
He took a slow breath.

"I didn’t grow up in a sealed inheritance realm. There wasn’t one." He said it evenly. "I came here from a lower-ranked world. It had a ceiling. I found a way past it and brought myself across, and everything I am was built there along a path that has nothing to do with roots or meridians or anything else in your library."
The water ran along its channel. Ji Liansu sat with her hands folded and said nothing for what felt like a considerable time.
"How long have you been in this world?" she asked.
"Less than two weeks."
Something moved behind her eyes then, and it was not doubt.

"That explains a great deal that has been bothering me since I read your record," she said. "You did not know what a Moonless was. You bought a children’s primer on meridians and understood half of it, which Elder Wen recorded because he thought it was a lie. Your circulation follows no route in any text I could name, and I could name several thousand." She tilted her head slightly. "And your age. Twenty-two, with that foundation—I had already decided the answer had to be a sealed realm with an extraordinary inheritance and a great deal of time distortion. A foreign path in a thin world is simpler and fits better."
"You believe me."

"I believe the version of you sitting in front of me makes more sense with this explanation than without it." She reached down and let two fingers rest in the running water. "A lower world. Energy-poor, I assume, by our standards. And you reached Peak Ascendant there, at twenty-two, and built a foundation my examiner could not map."
"It wasn’t easy."

"It was a gem buried where the surrounding earth could not feed it," Ji Liansu said. "That is not an insult to your home. A stone of that quality does not become less valuable for having formed in poor ground. It simply means nobody there ever saw what it could be, including, I suspect, you."
Leon had no answer for that, which she seemed to take as one.

"Your public history remains a collapsed inheritance realm," she said, withdrawing her hand and drying it on a cloth. "I will forbid further investigation into your origins, personally, and the Supreme Elders will accept that because they have to. I will not tell them what you have told me. Your former life and whatever you left in it are your own business."
"Why?"

"Because you told me without being made to." She set the cloth aside. "That is worth more to me than the information. I have taken disciples before who had to be opened like a locked chest. It is exhausting, and everything you learn that way is suspect."

Then her manner changed. It was not a large change — her posture stayed the same, her hands stayed folded — but the temperature of the room did something, and Leon found himself paying a great deal more attention than he had been.

"There is one thing I require," Ji Liansu said. "It is the only thing, and it is not negotiable. You are part of Jade Moon Palace now. I do not ask for devotion, and I do not care whether you ever come to feel anything for this place at all. Serve it honestly, learn from it, take what it can give you, and go as far as you can go. That is all I want."
"And if I betray it?"

"Then I will not forgive you," she said, in exactly the same tone she had used to discuss the water. "There will be no second conversation and no appeal. I say this once now so that you never have to wonder about it later."
Leon believed her completely.

That was the strange part. She had not raised her voice, released a scrap of pressure, or looked at him any differently. She was a slight woman sitting on a cushion in a plain room with a veil over the lower half of her face, and he understood with total clarity that if he ever gave her cause, she would end him between one breath and the next and think about something else afterward.

"I have no intention of betraying the Palace," he said. "I came here for knowledge and for strength. Everything I want is on the other side of learning what this world already knows. Selling that out would be stupid before it was anything else."
Ji Liansu considered him.
"An honest reason," she said. "Honest reasons hold better than noble ones. Very well."
She rose, and Leon rose with her.
"Now," she said. "Before you can improve, you need to understand what you are currently doing wrong."

chapters.title: Chapter 622: Power Before Cultivation
paragraphs: The practice chamber was built into the mountain, forty paces across, its walls covered in overlapping containment formations that Leon could feel breathing quietly against his perception.
"Nine," Ji Liansu said. "Small. Controlled. Show me each one, and show me only those nine."
Leon did as he was told, and did it well.

Fire came first: a fist-sized sphere hovering a meter off the floor, its surface perfectly still, holding the exact shape he had given it without flickering once. Water next, a rotating disc of it, edge-on. Earth rose from the stone floor in a smooth column and stopped where he stopped it. Wind ran a circuit around the chamber without disturbing a hair. Lightning arrived instantly, forked once, and held. Ice grew from nothing into a lattice of six repeating arms. Light stayed exactly as bright as he wanted it, edge-defined, no bleed. Darkness formed a contained sphere that swallowed the Light beside it and did not spread a finger’s width past its boundary.
Space he demonstrated by folding a corner of the chamber and putting his hand through it to touch the far wall.
Ji Liansu watched all nine without a word.

"Your skill execution is exceptional," she said finally. "I want that stated plainly, because everything I say afterward will sound like criticism and none of it is about your technique. Your control is better than any disciple on this peak. Your Space work is better than several elders’."
"But."
"But watch."
She raised one hand and produced a sphere of water.

It was the same size as his, spun at the same rate, held the same shape. Leon put his perception on it immediately and felt the difference before he understood it: her sphere sat in the air as though the air had agreed to hold it. His had been an argument he was winning.
"Match it," she said. "Both of us hold. We stop when one of us needs to add power."
Leon put his water back up and held it.

Two minutes passed. Three. At four, he felt the first small slippage — the sphere’s outer layer beginning to lose coherence — and he fed it, a light touch, hardly anything. At six he did it again. At nine minutes the corrections had become continuous, small and constant, like a man keeping a coin balanced on its edge with tiny movements of the finger.
Ji Liansu’s sphere had not changed at all. She had put nothing into it since it formed.
"Stop," she said.
Leon let his fall. It broke on the floor in a splash. Hers rose, unhurried, back to her palm and vanished.
"How much did you spend?" she asked.
"More than you."

"Four to five times more. Possibly six." She turned her hand over. "And this is what I want you to understand: my skill is not better than yours. If we were both handed identical energy at the same instant and told to make a sphere, yours would be at least as good as mine, and your Space is unquestionably better."
"Then what’s the difference?"
"The energy went into my technique already prepared," she said. "You put raw power into a perfect result and made the result do the work of refining it."
She walked to the wall and set her palm flat against the stone.

"A native cultivator has three stages before the technique ever happens. The spiritual root draws in what is around us and converts it — that is the first filter, and it is where impurity is removed. The meridians circulate it, and circulation is not transport. Every pass conditions the energy and conditions the channel. A method that runs a route ten thousand times leaves both the energy and the body changed." She turned back. "And the cultivation technique itself is the instruction for all of it — which routes, in which order, at what pressure, toward what quality. By the time a Dao Palace expert throws a flame, that flame is receiving fuel that has been refined specifically to become flame."
"And I’m pouring in whatever’s in the tank."

"You are pouring in something extraordinary that has never been refined for any purpose at all, and then compensating with precision so fine that it usually works." Ji Liansu’s tone stayed level. "It has kept you alive. I have read what you did in that merchant’s garden, and a Peak Ascendant has no business doing it. Your method is not stupid. It is expensive."
"How expensive?"

"You waste power on every single technique you use. You generate internal strain that a properly circulated cultivator does not, and you will feel that strain accumulate over decades even if you never notice it in a day. And in a long engagement—an hour, six hours, a running fight across three days—your stability degrades while that of a native cultivator with comparable reserves degrades far more slowly." She let that sit. "Any Void Immortal who understood what you are would simply refuse to finish quickly."
Leon thought about the Moonless, which had been perfectly happy to prolong the hunt, and said nothing.

"Now the difficult part," Ji Liansu said. "Jade Moon Palace has no core inheritance suitable for a Ninefold Elemental Harmony Spiritual Root. We have never needed one. Every method in our vaults was built for two or three elements at most, and the finest of them are the narrowest." She looked at him. "And whatever you are actually carrying beyond the nine makes the problem worse, not better. Forcing one of our protected inheritances onto your foundation would either fail outright or take root badly, and a badly rooted core method is worse than none."
"So you’re not going to teach me one."
"I am going to give you the library."
She said it as though it were a small thing.

"General collections, all of them. Foundational texts, public methods, collected foreign techniques, elemental treatises, historical research, complete techniques up to and including your current realm, and every failed experiment we have ever bothered to keep — and we keep a great many, because failures are cheaper to store than successes. Only the named core inheritances stay closed to you."
Leon took a moment with that.
"And what do you want in exchange?"

"Three months," Ji Liansu said. "At the end of them, you will bring me a complete first-stage personal cultivation technique. Your own. Built to accept every element I know you possess, and structured so that it does not have to be torn down when you eventually admit to the rest."
"First stage only?"

"First stage only. You will not break through during this, and I am telling you now, clearly, so that you cannot later claim you misunderstood — do not force an advancement while you are experimenting on your own foundation. People die that way. Talented people die that way more often, because they get further before it goes wrong."
"And if I can’t do it in three months?"

"Then you will tell me why, and I will decide whether the reason is good." She moved toward the door. "I will not hover over you and I will not solve it for you. If I designed it, it would be my method wearing your name, and it would fit you the way somebody else’s boots fit. Come to me at the end and I will inspect what you have built."
At the threshold she stopped.
"Your talent bought you this opportunity," she said. "Talent by itself only makes the eventual failure more expensive, because more was spent getting there. Do not disappoint me."
Then she was gone, and Leon stood alone in a forty-pace practice chamber with the water still spreading across the floor where his sphere had broken.
Three months to build a path.

He turned the problem over and found, underneath the weight of it, something he had not felt in a long time. For years—through the tower, the classes, the reawakening, and the crossing—every step forward had been a matter of acquiring something that already existed. A skill, a rank, a relic, a level.
Nobody had ever asked him to construct an entire path from first principles. This time, there was no finished reward waiting for him. He would have to make the road before he could walk it.
If you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do that would help me a lot

"And the cultivation technique itself is the instruction for all of it — which routes, in which order, at what pressure, toward what quality.
By the time a Dao Palace expert throws a flame, that flame is receiving fuel that has been refined specifically to become flame."
"And I’m pouring in whatever’s in the tank."
"You are pouring in something extraordinary that has never been refined for any purpose at all, and then compensating with precision so fine that it usually works." Ji Liansu’s tone stayed level.
"It has kept you alive.
I have read what you did in that merchant’s garden, and a Peak Ascendant has no business doing it.
Your method is not stupid.
It is expensive."
"How expensive?"
"You waste power on every single technique you use.
You generate internal strain that a properly circulated cultivator does not, and you will feel that strain accumulate over decades even if you never notice it in a day.

And in a long engagement—an hour, six hours, a running fight across three days—your stability degrades while that of a native cultivator with comparable reserves degrades far more slowly." She let that sit.
"Any Void Immortal who understood what you are would simply refuse to finish quickly."
Leon thought about the Moonless, which had been perfectly happy to prolong the hunt, and said nothing.
"Now the difficult part," Ji Liansu said.
"Jade Moon Palace has no core inheritance suitable for a Ninefold Elemental Harmony Spiritual Root.
We have never needed one.
Every method in our vaults was built for two or three elements at most, and the finest of them are the narrowest." She looked at him.
"And whatever you are actually carrying beyond the nine makes the problem worse, not better.
Forcing one of our protected inheritances onto your foundation would either fail outright or take root badly, and a badly rooted core method is worse than none."
"So you’re not going to teach me one."
"I am going to give you the library."
She said it as though it were a small thing.
"General collections, all of them.

Foundational texts, public methods, collected foreign techniques, elemental treatises, historical research, complete techniques up to and including your current realm, and every failed experiment we have ever bothered to keep — and we keep a great many, because failures are cheaper to store than successes.
Only the named core inheritances stay closed to you."
Leon took a moment with that.
"And what do you want in exchange?"
"Three months," Ji Liansu said.
"At the end of them, you will bring me a complete first-stage personal cultivation technique.
Your own.
Built to accept every element I know you possess, and structured so that it does not have to be torn down when you eventually admit to the rest."
"First stage only?"
"First stage only.

You will not break through during this, and I am telling you now, clearly, so that you cannot later claim you misunderstood — do not force an advancement while you are experimenting on your own foundation.
People die that way.
Talented people die that way more often, because they get further before it goes wrong."
"And if I can’t do it in three months?"
"Then you will tell me why, and I will decide whether the reason is good." She moved toward the door.
"I will not hover over you and I will not solve it for you.
If I designed it, it would be my method wearing your name, and it would fit you the way somebody else’s boots fit.
Come to me at the end and I will inspect what you have built."
At the threshold she stopped.
"Your talent bought you this opportunity," she said.
"Talent by itself only makes the eventual failure more expensive, because more was spent getting there.
Do not disappoint me."
Then she was gone, and Leon stood alone in a forty-pace practice chamber with the water still spreading across the floor where his sphere had broken.
Three months to build a path.
He turned the problem over and found, underneath the weight of it, something he had not felt in a long time.
For years—through the tower, the classes, the reawakening, and the crossing—every step forward had been a matter of acquiring something that already existed.
A skill, a rank, a relic, a level.
Nobody had ever asked him to construct an entire path from first principles.
This time, there was no finished reward waiting for him.
He would have to make the road before he could walk it.
If you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do that would help me a lot

chapters.title: Chapter 623: Granduncle Goes to the Library
paragraphs: Qingyue was waiting on the terrace, and she had clearly been practicing.
"Granduncle," she said. "The Palace Mistress has asked me to show you your residence and explain the rules."
Two disciples in pale grey were sweeping the terrace eleven paces away. Both of them stopped sweeping.
"That’s a new title," Leon said.
"It is the correct one." Her expression was flawless. "My master addressed you as Junior Uncle. That places you one generation above me. Anything else would be improper."
"Anything else."
"Anything else, Granduncle."
He let the silence run for exactly as long as it took the two sweeping disciples to look at each other.
"Lead on," he said, and Qingyue turned so quickly that her sleeve snapped.
They took the mountain path down the seaward side. She did not speak again until the terrace was well out of sight and there was nobody within four hundred paces in any direction.
"If you enjoy that," she said, "I will push you off this path."
"I’m enjoying it a normal amount."
"You are enjoying it a great deal more than a normal amount, Leon."
"I’m twenty-two."

"I amawareof how old you are. Half the Palace has spent the morning inventing ages for you, and none of them are entitled to the correct one." She kept walking. "I have served Jade Moon longer than you have been alive several times over. I have never once been outranked by a man who does not know what a Moonless is."
"I know what one is now."
"You know it because I cut it off your shadow."

The residence sat on Ji Liansu’s own peak, a quarter of the way up the eastern face and screened from the main terraces by a shoulder of rock: a walled compound with a main hall, two side buildings, a training yard, and a garden with an old plum tree in it. Small, by the standards of what he had seen this morning. Extremely well placed.
Leon felt the formations from thirty paces out and stopped counting layers at seven.

"Defensive, privacy, communication, and a cultivation array under the main hall floor," Qingyue said. "The last one is worth more than the building. It concentrates ambient energy and holds it steady, which matters when you are doing anything delicate." She led him through the gate. "Now listen carefully, because I am only explaining this once and you will need it."
She was brisk and thorough and better at this than he expected.

The token first — a flat disc of pale green jade with a single character on it, which he was to carry at all times and never lend. It opened the general library, the outer and middle terraces, four of the six training grounds, the medicine court’s public wing, and the requisition hall. It did not open the peaks of individual Supreme Elders, the inner training waters, or anything belonging to a named core inheritance.

The allowance came next: a monthly figure in spirit stones that made Leon do the arithmetic twice against Moonfall prices, plus a standing entitlement to request materials for research through the requisition hall, subject to review by nobody at all except Ji Liansu.

"Understand what you have been given," Qingyue said. "The stones are generous. They are not the point. There are core disciples on this mountain who have waited eighty years for permission to request restricted materials without a sponsor, and you may do it tomorrow, because your master is the Palace Mistress and nobody will ask her twice." She looked at him sideways. "Several people are going to be extremely jealous. Bear it politely."
"Noted."

"Conduct. You do not fight other disciples on Palace ground. You do not enter another elder’s peak without invitation. You do not discuss the examination record — that order came from the Palace Mistress and it is not decorative. If an elder makes you an offer of instruction, you may accept or decline freely; you belong to your master’s line and no one else can claim you."
"And attendants?"

Qingyue’s step did not change. "Direct disciples may sponsor personal attendants. Registration goes through the outer administration hall under your token, and the Palace expects you to be responsible for anyone you bring in. Most senior disciples keep one or two. Some keep a dozen and are considered ridiculous."
Four,Leon thought, and filed the whole thing away without a flicker. "Good to know."

She stayed another hour, showing him where things were and how the requisition forms worked, and left before midday with a final, immaculate, "Granduncle" delivered at the gate in front of the two service disciples who had carried up his allowance.
He spent the next two hours going over the residence with Space.

He found the seven formation layers he had expected and an eighth he had not, which turned out to be a slow-burning array under the garden that fed the plum tree. He traced every thread out of the compound: two ran to the peak’s central array and carried structural status, one carried the communication link, and one — the interesting one — ran to a monitoring station and would report a large hostile energy release or a breach of the outer wall.
Nothing listened. Nothing watched. He checked three times and then checked the boundary stones themselves, because a formation was only as honest as its anchors.
Clean.

He did not open the connection. Understanding the formations was the first half of the problem; the second half was knowing whether anyone ever came up here to inspect them, and he had been in this residence for four hours.
Not yet.
Then he went to the library.

It was not a building. It was a system of buildings, cut into the mountain across five levels and joined by covered stairs, and the general collections alone took him forty minutes to walk without stopping to read anything.

Cultivation methods from basic body preparation upward, shelf after shelf. An entire hall of techniques collected from factions Jade Moon had absorbed or defeated, catalogued by origin, some of them the last surviving copy of a family’s whole legacy. Studies of unusual spiritual roots — three rooms of those. Elemental treatises. A long low chamber of incomplete and abandoned experimental paths, the shelves visibly less worn than everywhere else.
Two sealed doors, each with a name on it, each closed to his token exactly as Ji Liansu had said.
He took down a text meant for eleven-year-olds and started there.

It was calledOpening the Twelve, and it explained the ordinary meridian sequence in the patient, repetitive way of a book written for children with no capacity for damage. Leon read it in under an hour and understood perhaps two-thirds.
Then the System did something new.
[New category established: Cultivation Techniques]
Opening the Twelve — Foundational
Compatibility: Unassessed
Comprehension: 14%
Circulation: Not attempted
Leon looked at that for a long moment.
Fourteen percent.

He had memorized the entire text. He could recite it. And the System, which had always handed him skills at maximum proficiency the moment he touched them, had looked at what was actually inside his head and given him fourteen percent.

So this doesn’t work like the rest of it.Which was, he decided, exactly right. Knowing the words was not knowing the road, and no number of them would ever move energy through a channel that did not exist yet.
He put the primer back and walked to the elemental halls, and stood at the end of a row that ran forty paces into the mountain.
Nine elements had been revealed. He intended to read every path in this building.

chapters.title: Chapter 624: A Thousand Roads That Cannot Meet
paragraphs: By the second day the library staff had stopped asking whether he needed anything and started simply leaving it.

Food arrived twice a day on a lacquered tray, and by the third day the trays had improved considerably. On the fourth, one of them came with a small covered dish of candied plum that nobody had mentioned and that was very good.
He noticed the delivery duty had become competitive around the same time.

The first few volunteers had been junior disciples who set the tray down, bowed to the floor, and fled. Now they arrived in twos and threes, and lingered by the shelf ends, and conducted extremely quiet conversations at a distance of about fifteen paces before leaving.
Leon caught fragments over the days, because he was not deaf and they were not as quiet as they believed.
—the bells, all nine, my senior sister was on the west terrace and she saw the pillar—
—younger than half the outer court, they say—
—nobody knows his age, the record’s sealed—
—came out of a collapsed realm somewhere in the Marches, no clan, nothing—
—he’s been in here five days. Does he sleep?

Nobody approached him. It stayed at admiration and curiosity and a certain amount of scheduling, and once a young disciple bowed so deeply on delivering the tray that she knocked her own forehead on the shelf, went crimson, and had to be walked out by a friend.
Leon thanked them politely, ate what he was given, and read.
He read every element the Palace had. He read the nine the monument had revealed and the ones it had not, mixing the latter among the rest so that no single subject stood out on any day’s shelf.

Beyond the elements, he read the connective material, which turned out to matter more: neutral circulation methods that carried no elemental character at all, body-and-spirit harmonization studies, weapon-oriented paths that shaped energy toward a blade or a spear rather than a phenomenon, healing systems built on entirely different assumptions, and three shelves of failed multi-affinity experiments that had been kept because somebody sensible had understood their value.
By the fifth day he had memorized several dozen complete techniques, and the System had a great deal to say about them.
Nine-Turn Cinnabar Furnace — Complete, Fire
Compatibility: High
Comprehension: 61%
Circulation: Not attempted
Still Lake Reflection — Complete, Water
Compatibility: High
Comprehension: 58%
Circulation: Not attempted
Deep Root Bearing Method — Complete, Earth
Compatibility: Moderate
Comprehension: 44%
Circulation: Not attempted
The numbers moved when he actually understood something and refused to move when he merely remembered it, which he found bracing.
Late on the fifth day, the real problem came into focus.

Every complete cultivation method did the same five jobs. It drew ambient energy in. It filtered that energy through the spiritual root. It circulated the result along a specific set of channels in a specific order. It conditioned the body and the foundation through repetition. And it delivered a refined product shaped for the kind of technique the method existed to serve.
The trouble was the third job.
Every one of them thinks its route is the only route.

The Cinnabar Furnace ran hot. It did not merely carry fire — it widened and heated the channels it used, deliberately, over years, because a channel that had been conditioned by fire carried fire better. It said so on the fourth page, proudly.

The ice methods wanted the opposite. Narrow channels. Cold and dense. One of them contained an explicit warning against practicing any yang-natured method alongside it, and listed the symptoms of trying.

The earth paths built weight and stability into the circulation, slow and enormously durable, and they were fundamentally incapable of the rapid state changes that wind and lightning methods took for granted. He found a wind manual that required a full-body transition four times per breath. He found an earth manual that considered a full transition per hour to be hasty.

And Space was worse than all of them. Every spatial method he could find demanded specific anchor points held in a specific relationship — and other methods ran their circulation straight through those positions without knowing or caring.
He sat with the whole map of it for most of an afternoon.

I can’t stack them.Nine complete techniques laid side by side would not become a ninefold method. They would become nine sets of contradictory instructions fighting over the same body, and the foundation underneath would be asked to satisfy conditions that cancelled each other out. The Cinnabar Furnace and the ice path alone would ruin him inside two years.
So the complete structures are the wrong thing to take.
What he actually needed was underneath them — the principle each method had discovered, separated from the exclusive architecture built around it.
That was a much harder problem, and it was at least the correct one.
On the sixth day he found the previous bearer.

The records sat in the third root-study chamber under a catalogue heading that translated roughly asirregular constitutions, historical, and they were not an inheritance. Leon had half-hoped for one and was almost relieved to be wrong.

What survived was a personal collection: four fragmentary journals, a bundle of separate elemental studies in the same hand, and a set of loose correspondence. The name on them was Yan Zhuo. The oldest record was more than three thousand years old.
He read every page through the seventh day.

The journals were a record of failure. Yan Zhuo had tried the obvious thing first, which was to master nine established methods in sequence, and had spent decades discovering what Leon had approached from the outside. He had then tried a rotation—running each element’s method in a strict cycle so no two ever conditioned the channels at once—and abandoned it after nearly a century, because a body could not be reconditioned nine ways forever and the rotation had begun to leave permanent damage.

What he settled on eventually was specific to himself. His body had an unusual quality the journals described obliquely and never fully explained, and half his solutions leaned on it. Leon read those sections twice and got nothing he could use.

But the principles were there, scattered through three thousand years of dust. How to test a route without committing to it. Which conditions were genuinely incompatible and which merely looked that way. A long, careful argument about why elemental purity was overrated and coordination was underrated, written by a man who had clearly lost that argument with somebody important.
And a line near the end of the fourth journal that Leon read four times:
I have spent two centuries learning nine languages and I still cannot say one sentence in all of them at once.
Yan Zhuo had reached Heaven Immortal in the end, but only after centuries of work. The journals made it clear that the root had given him compatibility and nothing else whatsoever.
On the eighth day, Leon read for somebody other than himself.
He worked through it carefully and gave each of them options rather than an answer, because he did not intend to hand four people a decision that had to be theirs.

For Seraphine he pulled three: a lightning circulation from an absorbed northern sect that emphasized tempo and recovery over raw output, a light-natured protective method built around a sword-bearer’s stance, and a general sword-cultivation path old enough to be public everywhere.

For Ira, four, all of them concerned with compression and delivery — fire methods that treated the body as a barrel rather than a bonfire, one weapon-circulation study on driving heat through a spear point without destroying the spear, and a technique for stopping.

For Vyra he chose differently. Endurance methods. A flame path built for holding a line rather than breaking one, from a lineage that had guarded a mountain pass for six hundred years, and two studies on coordinated cultivation among linked practitioners.
For Loriel: life and plant methods, three of them, and a gentle body-spirit harmonization course meant for physicians rather than fighters.

Not one of them came from a sealed door. Every method he selected was public, collected, extinct-lineage, or so widely circulated that a competent wanderer from anywhere could plausibly have picked it up.
That evening he walked out of the library at dusk carrying nothing at all.
No books. No copied slips. Nothing in his sleeves but a jade token and the whole of it sitting behind his eyes, word for word.

For Seraphine he pulled three: a lightning circulation from an absorbed northern sect that emphasized tempo and recovery over raw output, a light-natured protective method built around a sword-bearer’s stance, and a general sword-cultivation path old enough to be public everywhere.

For Ira, four, all of them concerned with compression and delivery — fire methods that treated the body as a barrel rather than a bonfire, one weapon-circulation study on driving heat through a spear point without destroying the spear, and a technique for stopping.
For Vyra he chose differently.
Endurance methods.

A flame path built for holding a line rather than breaking one, from a lineage that had guarded a mountain pass for six hundred years, and two studies on coordinated cultivation among linked practitioners.
For Loriel: life and plant methods, three of them, and a gentle body-spirit harmonization course meant for physicians rather than fighters.
Not one of them came from a sealed door.
Every method he selected was public, collected, extinct-lineage, or so widely circulated that a competent wanderer from anywhere could plausibly have picked it up.
That evening he walked out of the library at dusk carrying nothing at all.
No books.
No copied slips.
Nothing in his sleeves but a jade token and the whole of it sitting behind his eyes, word for word.

chapters.title: Chapter 625: A Foundation Without Walls
paragraphs: The residence appeared exactly as Leon had left it. He spent the next hour making certain appearances were not deceiving him.

All eight formation layers were present and unaltered. The four threads running out of the compound carried exactly what they had during his first inspection, and the boundary stones remained untouched. He checked the plum tree’s array, the training yard, the roof beams, and the floor of the main hall. Nothing anywhere in the residence had been added, moved, or awakened since his first inspection.
Only after satisfying himself did he begin copying.

For the next two days, Leon reconstructed the selected manuals from memory. He preserved their original names and publicly known origins so his companions would have plausible answers if anyone questioned them. What he removed were Jade Moon catalogue numbers, archive notes, and anything revealing where his copies had come from. He added his own observations in the margins and wrote a separate guide to the Palace’s ranks, forms of address, and basic customs.

When the last stack was ready, he built his own isolation inside the main hall: a self-contained spatial shell seated within the walls, drawing on nothing of theirs and pressing against nothing. He stood in the middle of it until he was certain the room could not be heard from outside.
Only then did he open the connection.

The portal lasted four seconds. He chose the exit point carefully—Xyra’s quarantine plot in the eastern flats, three hundred paces from the nearest cultivated field and already enclosed by layered barriers. The bundle of rewritten manuals dropped onto the bare soil. Leon closed the portal immediately and spoke to the women through their existing connection, which required no physical opening at all.

"There are several options suited to each of you, plus six general circulation texts everyone should read," he said. "Nothing in there is a Jade Moon inheritance. Every one of them is public, collected, or from a lineage that died out. If anyone ever asks where you learned it, the answer is boring."
"How much time do we have?" Seraphine asked.
"A little under three months out here. Which is—"
"More than two years inside," Vyra said. "Give or take."
"Give or take."

He laid out the rest while they read. Each of them was to test her options rather than commit to the first one that worked. They would choose the method that accepted a foreign foundation with the least resistance, grow auxiliary channels slowly under Loriel’s eye, and reach the point where drawing and circulating this world’s energy felt ordinary rather than like an achievement.

"And all of you need to learn to be smaller than you are," Leon said. "Publicly, you’re wandering cultivators who picked up decent methods and worked hard. Not one of you ever mentions a class. Not one of you fights at full output where anyone can see. Assume any elder who examines you properly can tell more than you want them to."
"Then the cover," Seraphine said. "Say it now, because I’ve been building objections since you left us, and I’d like to know which ones still apply."

"When you’re ready, I travel to a large city—somewhere busy enough that four capable people appearing is unremarkable. You arrive there separately. I take you on openly as personal attendants and register you under my token. Then we return through the front gate in daylight with paperwork."
"Roles?"
"You’re chief attendant and personal guard. Ira is my combat guard. Vyra is my steward and adviser. Loriel manages the medicinal garden."
There was a pause.
"Combat guard," Ira said. "That’s what it says? On a form?"
"On a form."
"That’s the most respectable thing anyone has ever accused me of. I’m going to be insufferable about it."
"You’re going to bequietabout it," Vyra said, "which is the actual problem."

Her voice became more serious when she addressed Leon. "We have enough time to learn the circulation. What gets us caught is a woman who bows wrong, uses the wrong word for a senior, or doesn’t know that you don’t step onto another elder’s peak. I found your guide on manners and seniority. I’ll drill all four of us, but send anything else you learn."
"I will."
"Good."

"Leon." Loriel spoke carefully. "These life methods. The third one is—" She stopped. "It’s very good. Whoever wrote it understood something about how a body wants to heal that I’ve never seen written down anywhere."
"Then use it. And Loriel—"
"I know," she said more quietly. "Nobody sees what I actually am. I know."
"Not forever. Just until I understand what these people do with someone like you."
Seraphine’s voice came last, after the others had returned to their reading.
"You sound better," she said.
"I’m being taught. It’s been a while."
"Then let her teach you." She paused. "And come back."
He closed the connection, released his isolation, and left the Palace’s formations exactly as they had been issued.
Leon returned to the library the next morning and spent four more days refining his design. On the last of them, he understood that he had been building the wrong thing from the beginning.

By then, the design covered two tables: nine routes, one for each public element, each stripped down to its underlying principle and rebuilt from scratch so that no channel became conditioned against another. It was elegant. He had solved the conflict between heat and cold with a shared neutral segment. He had given Space its anchor points without letting the earth circulation cross them. Counting his earlier research, it represented nearly two weeks of good work, and it was very close to functioning.
He was checking the sixth route against the second when one thought brought the entire design down.
Nine.
Nine routes. Nine channels. A structure built to hold exactly nine things and no more.
I’m making another monument.

The stone in the examination hall had been an excellent artifact. It had reached into him honestly, found nine compatibilities, filled nine sockets, and stopped because nine was all its makers had thought to provide. Three thousand years ago, none of them had considered that someone might arrive with more.

Leon was about to impose the same limitation upon himself. He would spend three months constructing a beautiful nine-route foundation while every affinity he still concealed remained outside it with nowhere to go. The first time he tried to bring another one in, he would have to tear down the whole structure and rebuild it with ten routes. Then eleven. Then however many came after that.
Leon sat back and looked at two tables of excellent work.
The number is the mistake. Any number is the mistake.

What he needed was not a collection of routes. He needed a center—a framework within his foundation that carried no elemental character at all. It would take in energy of any kind, refine it, condition it, and pass it onward without caring what it was. Individual elemental principles could connect to that center, feed from it, and return to it, but none of them would own it or change its fundamental nature.
If he added a tenth element, nothing would need to be rebuilt. The new path would simply attach to what was already there.

He sat with the idea for a long time, searching for the flaw, and found several. He had no idea how to create a circulation that refined energy without shaping it toward something. Every neutral method he had studied was neutral only because it was weak. His center would have to be stronger than anything he possessed, yet he had not worked out what it would be made from. Nothing in the Palace archive described such a framework ever existing.
It was a much harder problem than nine routes.
It was also the right one.
He gathered every page of the nine-route design, stacked them, and set them aside rather than destroying them. Parts of the abandoned design would survive into whatever came next.
Then he took out a blank sheet and drew a single circle in its center, with nothing attached and no number written anywhere.
He still had most of his three months. For the first time since Ji Liansu had closed the practice chamber door behind her, Leon knew what he was actually trying to build.

chapters.title: Chapter 626: Too Much for the First Step
paragraphs: The new design took six days and covered most of the main hall’s floor.

Leon rewrote it four times. What survived would not have been recognized as a cultivation technique by anyone in the library. It possessed no elemental character, used no scriptural language, and promised nothing about what it would eventually produce.
It was simply a route.

Energy entered through the lower channels, completed a circuit through the trunk of his body, passed into a central section built to belong to nothing, and returned along a path that ended where it had begun.

That central section was the entire idea. Every complete method in the Palace conditioned its channels toward the type of power it existed to create. Leon’s route had to remain neutral after Fire passed through it, then Water, then every affinity he was still hiding from the Palace.
The System could identify his problems. It offered no solutions.
[Cultivation Technique — Unnamed, Personal]
Structure: Incomplete
Unresolved structural points: 6
Circulation: Not attempted
Compatibility: Unassessed

The assessment remained unchanged every time he checked. It counted the problems he already knew existed while declining to tell him what belonged in those places. After the third day, Leon stopped hoping it would do more and returned to solving them himself.
On the seventh day, he sent word to Ji Liansu that he was ready to test the route.

The chamber she gave him was cut deep into her personal peak. It measured twenty paces across, and its walls had been built in three shells of containment work, with a channel of running water around the outer edge. Whatever went wrong inside would remain inside.
Ji studied his diagrams while he waited. She took long enough that Leon resisted the urge to speak twice.

"I find no theoretical conflict," she said at last. "The neutral section is unusual, but I cannot immediately say that it will fail. Your junction placement is sound, and your return path is exceptionally well constructed."
She set the pages down.
"Understand precisely what I have told you. The design contains no error I can identify on paper."
"That’s not the same as safe."

"It is not remotely the same as safe. A cultivation route is more than a diagram or formation. It is something you establish inside a living body that has never followed it before." Ji moved to the edge of the chamber. "Begin small and stop at anything that surprises you. I will be here."
Leon sat in the center of the floor and closed his eyes.

The first part came easily. Drawing energy inward was something his body had done since the moment he arrived in this world, and the ambient power surrounding Ji Liansu’s peak was thick enough to feel against his skin. He gathered a small amount within his lower channels and held it there.
Now guide it in.

He knew the quantity he wanted. Years of practice had taught him exactly how much energy any given task required, and this was a small task—a first attempt using a fraction of what he would have committed to the simplest technique he possessed.
By every standard he had relied upon for years, he was being extremely conservative.
He moved the energy.
The first section of the route did not open. It tore.

Pain struck before he understood what had happened. White pressure split upward through his chest and spread along both arms as the energy entered a channel that had never carried anything. Instead of widening slowly over years of cultivation, the channel was forced open in an instant. Leon felt its wall give way, followed by something deeper behind it.
Stop. Reduce.
He tried to pull the energy back and discovered that it was no longer entirely under his control.

The half-formed route had begun drawing power on its own. Ambient energy poured toward the tear, feeding the surge. The surge widened the opening, and the larger opening drew in even more. Pressure climbed inside his chest. His ribs creaked. Blood rose into his mouth, and he swallowed it as he worked.
The shape of the problem was clear enough: close the intake, release pressure through the second junction, and seal the wall behind it.
None of those solutions were working fast enough.
An ordinary beginner would already have lost consciousness. The first rupture would have overwhelmed them, and their body would have shut itself down before the damage could spread.
Leon’s body refused to grant him that protection. It held together, kept him conscious, and allowed the energy to continue ripping through pathways he had spent six days designing.
The containment shells began to hum.
Then the ambient energy in the chamber vanished.

It did not drain away or gradually fade. It ceased to exist as something the damaged route could reach. An absolute seal closed over the chamber, cutting off everything outside Leon’s body. At the same moment, the energy escaping through his skin was forced back down and contained.
That’s her.
Ji Liansu had cut off the fuel and closed the leak. The unstable circulation inside him, she left in his hands.

Leon stopped trying to control the entire route and dealt with it in pieces. He choked the intake. He deliberately collapsed the third junction, which hurt worse than the original tear, then bled the remaining pressure slowly along a return path that had also been damaged.
It took nearly two minutes.
When it ended, Leon was on his hands and knees, staring at his blood on the stone.

Light gathered around his hands without being summoned. He let it work. Torn channels closed, ruptured vessels sealed, and the deep bruising across his chest faded over the next dozen breaths. By the time he sat upright, nothing remained physically wrong with him.
Ji Liansu had not moved from the wall.
"You didn’t heal me," Leon said.
"You do it better than I would, and considerably faster. There is no virtue in a master performing a task badly merely to appear attentive."
She came forward and crouched, examining the residue hanging in the air above the floor with two fingers held apart.
"Tell me what you did wrong."
"The design—"
"The design is intact. Look at it properly."
Leon did. He opened the System’s record and found the answer waiting in plain sight.
[Circulation Attempt — Failed]
Rupture points: 14
Primary cause: Intake volume exceeded pathway tolerance at section one
Secondary damage: Cascade from primary rupture
Fourteen tears. Thirteen were consequences. Only one was the original mistake.
"How much did you use?" Ji asked.
"A fraction of what I’d put into a small technique."
"Yes. And how much had you cultivated before today?"
Leon fell silent.

"You possess the raw power of a Peak Golden Core cultivator," Ji said. "It is genuine. I do not know how you acquired it, and this morning it nearly crippled you. Whatever your strength, you have never completed a single cultivation circulation in your life. Your body is extraordinary, but the pathways cultivation actually uses are those of a child who has not begun."
"So a fraction of my strength—"

"Was perhaps forty times what that channel could survive." She stood. "This is what your durability conceals from you. An ordinary beginner cannot make this mistake because his body faints and saves him. Yours will let you continue while you destroy yourself, and it will make you believe you are managing the damage."
"And if I’d forced it open anyway?"

"Then the route would work," Ji said, her voice level. "That is what makes forcing it tempting. A damaged channel still carries energy, but it also carries the scar. The scar becomes a habit, and the habit becomes part of the shape of your circulation forever. At Golden Core, you would notice nothing. At Nascent Soul, it would cost you a little. Somewhere in the immortal realms, that weakness would split open under pressure at the worst possible moment, and you would not understand why."
She looked down at him.
"I have seen what follows. The damage does not always kill quickly, and by then repairing the foundation may be harder than rebuilding it."
Leon absorbed that.
"You’re not telling me to stop."

"No. Your design is good, and your instinct concerning the neutral section may be genuinely original." Ji moved toward the door. "You will rebuild the circulation around the smallest quantity of energy you can meaningfully control. Not a small quantity by your standards—the smallest amount you can still feel and direct. Begin where a child of nine begins, and do not concern yourself with what you already are."
She paused at the threshold.
"Everything that happened today can be traced to one decision. You tried to make your body catch up to your strength in a single step. It cannot. Nothing can."

"You will rebuild the circulation around the smallest quantity of energy you can meaningfully control.
Not a small quantity by your standards—the smallest amount you can still feel and direct.
Begin where a child of nine begins, and do not concern yourself with what you already are."
She paused at the threshold.
"Everything that happened today can be traced to one decision.
You tried to make your body catch up to your strength in a single step.
It cannot.
Nothing can."

chapters.title: Chapter 627: Healing Was Not the Point
paragraphs: Leon returned to his residence in Jade Moon Palace, checked every formation, and raised his private spatial isolation. Once he was certain no one could observe him, he opened a portal into the dimensional world and stepped through.
He emerged in the study, intending to collect a clean set of clothes and see how the others were progressing with their manuals.
Seraphine looked up from her reading. The moment she saw him, her expression changed.
"That’s blood."
Leon glanced down. The robe had dried stiff across the chest and both sleeves, and he had entirely stopped noticing it somewhere in the last two hours.
"It’s mine," he said, "and it’s old. First cultivation attempt went badly. I healed it before I left the chamber."

He explained the rest while searching for a clean set—the neutral route, the mistake with the intake, the fourteen tears, and Ji sealing the room. He kept it brief and accurate, the way he would have reported it to Kaela. When he finished, he turned around expecting to discuss the redesign.
Seraphine was standing very still.
"Fourteen," she said.
"They were internal. Nothing structural. The Light closed all of it inside a minute—"
"Stop talking."
He stopped.
"You just told me that you tore open fourteen places inside your own body," she said, "in the tone of a man describing a delivery that arrived late."
"Because that’s what it was. An experiment that failed, with a cause I understand, which I’m not going to repeat—"
"Leon." Her voice did not rise, which was worse. "Do you know how long it has been since you talked about your own body as something that can be hurt?"
He opened his mouth and found nothing in it.

"You heal," Seraphine said. "You’ve always healed. Every wound you’ve taken since the Tower has closed inside a minute, and somewhere in the last few years you stopped counting them. Now you make decisions as if you’re the one person in any room whose safety doesn’t have to be part of the calculation."
She stepped closer.

"You sent us inside so we’d be safe. You wouldn’t open the connection with the leopard’s mark on you because a door might endanger the city. You shielded four people through an entire fight and let a plate open your back doing it, and you didn’t mention it for three days. Every one of those decisions was correct. And every one of them treated Leon as the acceptable cost."
"That’s not—"

"It is exactly that. And it works because you can heal. Until the one time it’s something you can’t heal, and then it isn’t your problem anymore." Her jaw tightened. "It’s ours. You don’t get to be the one who dies and calls it efficient."
Behind her, Ira appeared in the doorway.
"Fourteen holes," Ira said. "You couldn’t stop at three?"
"Ira."

"I’m getting there." She came in and dropped onto the arm of a chair. The humor left her face entirely. "She’s right, and I’m going to say the same thing badly. I’ve spent more than three months learning a lightning method because you handed me a book, and the entire time I’ve been assuming that when this is finished, I’ll be standing next to you again. That’s the whole plan. That’s the only reason any of us are doing any of this."
She looked directly at him.
"So stop being casual about the part where you’re alive."
Vyra had appeared in the doorway as well, her arms folded.

"The experiment was correct," she said. "You had to test it, and there was no safe way to find out except by finding out. I’d have done the same." Her gaze moved to the ruined robe. "But you walked out of a room where you nearly crippled yourself, decided it was solved, and came here to change your shirt. That’s the part."
Loriel said nothing.

She had entered behind Vyra and was staring at the front of his robe with her hands pressed flat together. When Leon looked at her properly, she turned her face away and failed to hide any of what she felt.
That was what actually landed.
"All right," he said.
He sat down on the edge of the desk.

"This one was preventable. I know exactly what I did—I used what felt cautious to me, and cautious to me is forty times what a first circulation can survive." He looked at Seraphine. "I went into it confident because I’ve spent three years knowing I can repair anything that happens to me. That’s the honest version. I wasn’t brave. I was careless in a way I’ve stopped being able to notice."
"You’re not going to promise you’ll stay out of danger," Seraphine said.
"No. I’d be lying, and you’d know it."
"Good."

"What I’ll promise is procedure. Every test from here goes at a fraction I can feel, with the smallest workable increase, and I stop the moment anything reads as strain instead of resistance. Ji sits in the chamber for the dangerous ones. And when something goes wrong, I tell you the same day."
Seraphine held his gaze for a moment longer.
"Acceptable," she said, letting out a breath. "I’m still angry."
"I’d think less of you if you weren’t."
"Don’t be charming. It’s been a bad afternoon."

Leon stayed long enough to see where they were with the manuals, which turned out to be less far along than the noise in the study had suggested. Seraphine had eliminated one of her three options and was arguing with the other two. Ira had tried to run the compression method at full output on the second day and had been talked out of it by Vyra, who had spent most of her first week studying general circulation texts before touching an elemental path. Loriel had read all four of her methods twice and chosen none.
"They’re all wrong in different ways," Loriel said. "I need to feel one before I’ll know."
"Then take the time. You’ve got years in here."

Leon changed into the clean robe before leaving. Then he reopened the portal, stepped back into his residence at Jade Moon Palace, and sealed the dimensional passage behind him. After confirming that his private isolation remained undisturbed, he released it.
He rebuilt the route over the following four days, and the rebuild was not a repair. It was a different idea.

The first design had assumed he would establish the whole circulation at once and then refine it. That was how every complete method in the library described the process, because every complete method had been written for a body already conditioned by a preparatory course during childhood.
So Leon discarded that assumption. He would build one section at a time, using a thread of neutral energy so thin that his first attempt to gather it took nine minutes because he kept overshooting.
Ji gave him the chamber again. She remained by the wall and offered no instruction.

The first attempt dispersed at the second junction, which Leon had not known was possible. The second stalled halfway through a transition and remained there until he released it. The third returned along the wrong path and escaped somewhere through his left forearm, producing no damage and a great deal of useful information. The fourth failed for a reason he did not identify for two hours. The seventh went most of the way before simply thinning out, like water sinking into sand.
None of them hurt. That was the strangest part. After fourteen ruptures, failing quietly felt like nothing at all.
Each failure went into the record, and the record began to prove useful.
[Circulation Attempt 11 — Failed]
Dispersal at junction 4
Transition angle inconsistent with sections 3 and 5
He corrected the angle. Attempt twelve failed somewhere else.
On the nineteenth attempt, the thread entered the first section and continued moving.

It traveled slowly enough for Leon to feel every part of the journey: the lift at the second junction, the long quiet stretch through his trunk, and the odd, weightless moment when the neutral section accepted the energy, held it, and returned it without adding anything. The thread entered the return path, reached the end that was also its beginning, and settled there.
One circulation. Complete.
It had required less energy than lighting a lamp.
Leon opened his eyes. Nothing visible had happened. There was no aura, pressure, light, or sensation of power anywhere in the chamber. Ji Liansu still stood against the wall with her hands folded.
He had carried enough force to kill Void Immortals for weeks, yet none of it had ever felt like this.
That’s the first thing I’ve ever cultivated.
