You will begin there."
"Do they have anything related to the Earthmarrow fern?"
"Possibly.
You are not asking anyone about a rare plant connected to another world on your first day."
Loriel looked offended.
"I know that."
"You were about to ask."
"Only you."
By the time they finished, Vyra had filled twelve pages with terminology, hierarchy, forms of address, and the limits of Leon’s token.
She also insisted that everyone carry ordinary local clothing and possessions rather than items that might invite questions.
Preparing to leave made the decision real in a way the discussion had not.
Seraphine packed quickly and kept only what she could carry without a storage artifact.
Ira complained about wrapping her spear, then redid the cloth herself when the first covering looked too conspicuous.
Loriel spent nearly an hour arranging care for the quarantine plot and explaining the Earthmarrow fern’s schedule to three different gardeners.
Vyra checked all four sets of belongings before allowing anyone to close them.
Leon watched without hurrying them.
They had been ready in cultivation.
Leaving the place that had sheltered them was a different kind of preparation.
The following morning, Leon returned alone to Jade Moon Palace.
Ji Liansu received him in the same quiet hall where she had examined the first stage of his Scripture.
Her gaze passed once over his channels before settling on his face.
"You recovered quickly."
"The damage is closed.
I will not resume experimentation until the remaining strain fades."
"Good.
What do you need?"
Leon placed his direct-disciple token on the table between them.
"Four attendants connected to my sealed inheritance have reached a nearby port.
They survived the same secret realm and remained behind while I established a secure identity.
I want to register them under my token."
Ji Liansu knew that Leon came from a lower-ranked world.
She also knew the sealed-inheritance explanation protected facts he did not intend to share.
As she had promised before, she did not ask him to expose those facts now.
"Their cultivation?" she asked.
"All four are Peak Foundation Establishment.
Their methods are unusual but stable."
"Their roles?"
Leon listed them.
Ji Liansu considered the request for a moment, then touched one finger to the token.
A pale crescent appeared on its surface.
"This authorizes four personal attendants under your responsibility," she said.
"The gate officials will record their names, cultivation, and duties.
Their origins will be registered under the same sealed-realm protection as yours.
I will not permit anyone to investigate beyond that without bringing the request to me."
"Thank you."
"Do not thank me yet.
Their conduct will reflect on you, and yours will determine how closely the Palace watches them."
Leon thought of Ira asking whether she could fight anyone.
"Understood."
Ji Liansu’s eyes narrowed slightly.
"That answer lacked confidence."
"One of them is enthusiastic."
"Then I look forward to discovering whether your judgment is better in attendants than it is in duels."
Leon collected the token and left before she found another way to make the point.
By afternoon, he had descended to the nearest port under Jade Moon Palace authority and rented a small courtyard using his token.
He inspected every formation himself, added two seals of his own, and confirmed that the property possessed no hidden observation array.
Only then did he enter the dimensional world.
The four women were waiting with their belongings packed in plain local cloth.
Seraphine wore her sword openly.
Ira had wrapped her spear but looked tempted to remove the covering.
Vyra carried the book of notes beneath one arm, while Loriel held a small case of medicinal tools against her chest.
"Everything is approved," Leon said.
"You will be registered under my token, and Ji Liansu has extended my sealed-realm protection to your origins.
We appear in the port, walk to the Palace openly, and enter through the front gate."
Vyra nodded.
Ira straightened with immediate interest.
Loriel looked nervous but did not step back.
Seraphine came to Leon’s side.
"And after the gate?"
"After the gate, you stop waiting for my visits and live there with me."
Her expression softened.
Leon looked at all four of them.
They had crossed one world at his side, spent more than ten months building foundations for another, and reached the point he had once expected to take years.
"It is time," he said.
He opened the passage.
Cold, dense mana flowed into the dimensional world.
Beyond the full standing gateway waited the quiet courtyard of the port, its stone walls silver beneath the higher world’s moonlight.
No one crossed yet.
Together, they looked through.

chapters.title: Chapter 636: Five Names at the Gate
paragraphs: One of the public routes into Jade Moon Palace passed through its eastern harbor.

Three stone piers extended from the walled port into water clear enough that Leon could follow the anchor chains down forty feet. Supply barges came and went throughout the morning, along with passenger vessels carrying merchants, Palace disciples, and workers returning from the mainland.
Leon and the four women arrived aboard one of those passenger vessels and walked down the pier with their documents prepared.

"Formation seam at the second pier head," Seraphine said quietly, three steps behind his left shoulder. "There’s a gap in the outer array where the stone was repaired. They patched it with a secondary node instead of recutting the anchor."
"You’ve been here ninety seconds."
"It’s a bad patch."

Ahead, the pier opened into a receiving yard with checkpoint tables arranged beneath a broad awning. Vyra had stopped watching the water and begun studying how a clerk handled a merchant’s token. He examined it, compared it against one ledger, and then passed it to a second clerk who checked another record.
"Two independent checks," Vyra said. "Different books. Neither clerk can approve entry alone."
"Is that good?"

"It’s honest, which is more than I expected." Her attention shifted to the guards positioned around the inner arch. "Those two are Foundation Establishment. The man sitting down is Golden Core and pretending to be bored."
Ira had noticed none of it.

She was staring past the receiving yard toward the terraced mountainside, where sunlight flashed across a series of white platforms cut into the stone. Figures moved across them, accompanied by the distant flare of techniques being released and caught.
"Those are training grounds," she said.
"They are."
"There are eleven of them."
"Ira."
"I’m not saying anything." She turned and walked backward for several paces so she could continue watching. "I’m noting the number."
Loriel had stopped entirely.
She crouched beside a strip of silver-green growth planted along a formation channel, one finger hovering above a leaf without touching it.
"Young Master Leon, this was planted deliberately."
"Most gardens are."

"No. It was planted inside the channel." Loriel pointed toward the thin stream of spiritual energy escaping through the stone. "This species absorbs the overflow. Someone found the exact place where the array vents and chose a plant that could use what would otherwise be wasted."
She looked up with an expression Leon had rarely seen since their arrival in the higher world.
"That took someone a very long time to understand."
Ten months preparing out of sight, and they haven’t been in the open for half a morning.
He had not expected to enjoy this as much as he did.

The woman waiting at the checkpoint appeared to be around forty. She wore plain Palace grey, with an administrative seal hanging from her belt. Her cultivation sat quiet enough that only Leon’s senses caught its depth.
Late Nascent Soul.

"Senior Brother Leon." She bowed the proper amount. "Han Suwen, senior deacon of outer administration. The Palace Mistress assigned me to oversee your household’s registration. Your authority token, please."
Leon handed it over.
Han Suwen examined it properly. She turned it, checked the characters engraved on its face, and held it against the light to inspect the internal grain before returning it.
"You know who I am," Leon said.
"Everyone on this mountain knows who you are. That has nothing to do with whether the token in your sleeve is the one issued to you."
She turned toward the registration tables.

"Your household’s identities carry the Palace Mistress’s written authorization. That settles the question of their origin. Nobody here will ask them about the collapsed inheritance realm or demand to inspect what they brought from it."
"And what will they ask?"

"Cultivation, bone age, affinity, and whether any of them carries something capable of killing people on this mountain." Han Suwen glanced back. "Those checks apply to everyone entering through this gate, including elders returning from missions. I will not skip them because your master signed a document, and I will not extend them merely to prove that I cannot be influenced. Is that acceptable?"
"Entirely."
Vyra caught up with Leon as they followed Han Suwen.
"I like her," she said.
Registration took less than an hour, most of it spent waiting for the testing stations to clear.
The bone-age artifact was smaller than the monument used during Leon’s assessment, but it performed the same basic task. Four readings appeared. None caused concern.
The cultivation test used a shallow stone basin. Each woman placed her hand above its surface and circulated a measured amount of spiritual energy.
The answer appeared four times.
[Peak Foundation Establishment]
The clerk checked the second and third results twice before writing an additional note in his ledger.
"Their foundations are extremely stable," he reported to Han Suwen. "Far more than normal for recently registered cultivators."
"Record the observation and continue."
The affinity examination drew more attention.

Seraphine went first. Violet-white lightning appeared along one side of the formation plate while clean golden light emerged from the other. Rather than repelling each other, the two currents settled into a stable interwoven pattern.
The clerk consulted the reference beside him.
"Lightning and light," he said. "Both strong. Dual-affinity harmony in the upper range."
His attention lingered on the result, then shifted toward the cloth-wrapped sword on Seraphine’s back. Whatever conclusion he reached remained his own.
"Affinities recorded," Han Suwen said.
Ira and Vyra both registered as fire cultivators, yet the formation responded to them differently.

Ira’s flame gathered close to the plate, compact and bright, with almost no energy escaping from its core. Vyra’s spread evenly across the formation and remained under precise control. When it touched the residue Ira’s test had left behind, it folded the weaker flame into itself without losing stability.
The clerk stared for a moment before writing both results.
Loriel’s affinity caused him to call over a second official.
Wood and vitality filled the plate with a deep living green. The color continued strengthening long after an ordinary reading would have settled.
The second official watched for several breaths.
"What is your cultivation background?" he asked.
"Medicinal," Loriel said. "Mostly plants."
"Mostly plants," he repeated. "Young lady, your vitality affinity is purer than anything I’ve measured from the medicine court this year."
"Thank you."
He plainly wanted to ask more, but Han Suwen closed the matter.
"Affinities recorded. Continue."

Nobody asked to see a cultivation technique. Nobody demanded that Seraphine unwrap her sword or questioned how Ira compressed her fire. They verified identity, cultivation, affinities, stable circulation, and the absence of demonic corruption or possession.
Then the examination ended.

Leon had half expected someone to push beyond that boundary. Watching the officials stop exactly where their authority stopped told him more about Jade Moon Palace than several weeks in its library had.
The five of them attracted attention. That was unavoidable.

Four young Peak Foundation Establishment cultivators entering a single household drew notice in any receiving yard. By the time their tokens were being prepared, Leon counted eleven people who had found reasons to stand nearby.
The whispers began before the group was out of earshot.
"Four of them, all Peak Foundation..."
"The inheritance realm. There must have been other survivors."
"The ledger says attendants."
"Attendants," someone repeated, followed by quiet laughter.
One older disciple watched Seraphine rather than the others.
"That one isn’t an ordinary servant," he told his companion. "Look where she stands relative to him. That’s a guard’s position."

Nobody approached them or said anything openly disrespectful. The reaction remained what Leon had expected: curiosity, calculation, and the first pieces of a story that would reach every inhabited peak before evening.
Han Suwen completed the record and read the positions aloud.

"Seraphine, chief attendant and personal guard. Ira, combat guard. Vyra, steward and adviser. Loriel, medicinal-garden and spiritual-plant attendant. All four registered to the household of Leon, direct disciple of the Palace Mistress."
Their tokens were pale green, each bearing Leon’s household mark beneath the insignia of Jade Moon Palace.
With the registration complete, Han Suwen led them up the terraced road toward the front gate.
It stood thirty feet high and remained open beneath the daylight. Disciples, workers, merchants, and guards moved through in both directions.
Leon crossed it with the four women beside him.

For weeks, he had opened brief apertures from his sealed cultivation room to pass books and resources into the dimensional world. He had asked them to remain hidden and to make themselves smaller than they were because a single careless witness could expose everything.
Now they walked beside him on a public road, and the only thing following them was rumor.
This is how it should have been.

chapters.title: Chapter 637: The Peak Was Quiet Once
paragraphs: The road to Leon’s personal peak took nearly an hour, and Han Suwen answered questions throughout the climb.
"Can attendants use the combat grounds?" Ira asked less than five minutes after leaving the gate.
"Three of the eleven," Han Suwen replied. "The lower western platforms are open to household members and outer disciples. The others require disciple standing or an elder’s authorization."
"Can I challenge someone?"
"You may not issue challenges to ranked disciples. You may spar with anyone who agrees, and they may refuse without explanation."
"And if somebody challenges me?"
"You may accept. If you injure a core disciple, you will explain the circumstances to me, and I will record them accurately. That will help you less than you imagine."
Ira considered the answer.
"That’s fair."
"It is the rule. Fairness is a separate question."
Loriel asked about gardens.

Her household token granted access to the outer medicinal grounds and three public cultivation gardens. Restricted gardens, where the medicine court kept its rarer plants, required disciple standing or accumulated contribution.
"So I can earn access," Loriel said.

"You can. It will take time, and the medicine court is particular about whom it allows to work there." Han Suwen glanced at her. "It is also chronically short of people capable of keeping difficult plants alive. Make of that what you wish."

Vyra’s questions took longer. Han Suwen answered every one without suggesting that the list was excessive: supply accounts, monthly allowances, Palace-assigned staff, residence permissions, mission registration, contribution payments, and library access.
"Who maintains the formations around Leon’s peak?" Seraphine asked.

"The Palace. Four arrays rotate through the formation hall’s maintenance schedule. Two others are your master’s private work, and nobody touches them without permission." Han Suwen’s expression sharpened slightly. "Report any faults in the Palace arrays to me. Do not repair them yourself. The last disciple who improved a Palace formation without authorization spent a year hauling stone."
"Understood."
Halfway up, the road passed within sight of one of the western training platforms.
Two disciples were sparring with practice spears. Ira’s head turned and remained turned for the next eleven paces.
"You seem deeply unimpressed," Vyra said.
"Their footwork is wrong."
"Mm."
"It is. The taller one plants his rear foot before committing, so the thrust can be read half a beat early." Ira faced forward. "I was judging their form. Professionally."
"Of course."
Leon’s residence had a staff of nine responsible for the outer paths, delivery court, kitchens, guest rooms, and grounds beyond the inner wall.

They had spent the past month maintaining a residence for one man who was rarely in the building. Now they lined up in the front courtyard and bowed, visibly uncertain what to do with four additional household members.
The inner grounds operated differently.

Leon’s cultivation chambers remained sealed. The women’s quarters stood inside the protected boundary, and no outside staff member could enter without permission. Anything connected to the dimensional world, their Classes, or Leon’s deeper secrets would be discussed only inside those wards.
Vyra requested the staff list, supply records, access tokens, maintenance schedule, and household inventory within twenty minutes.
She found no corruption or sabotage. The residence had simply been established for one secluded disciple and had never been updated for anything else.

"There are two delivery-court tokens, and neither is listed in the residence ledger," she said. "The kitchen orders food for one person but has over-ordered rice for three weeks because nobody corrected the standing request. The eastern wall is inspected quarterly despite being the most recently repaired section."
She turned another page.
"The repair was handled by the same crew responsible for the seam Seraphine noticed at the harbor."
"Can you fix it?" Leon asked.
"Most of it within a week." Vyra continued reading. "Ira."
Ira had left two of her three bags beside the entrance and was already moving toward the door.
"I’m going to inspect the western platform."
"We have been inside this residence for eleven minutes."
"Plenty of time to inspect a platform."

"You left your luggage in the middle of a walkway. A servant moves it, a servant handles a combat guard’s equipment, and tomorrow I spend an hour explaining to Seraphine why an unvetted person touched your belongings." Vyra raised her eyes. "Take the bags."
Ira collected them, grumbling all the way to her quarters.
She returned three minutes later and left for the platform anyway.
Nobody stopped her.
Loriel discovered the inner garden and disappeared into it.

It was not ruined. It had been planted competently decades ago with species chosen almost entirely because they survived neglect: silver-thorn along the walls, two moon-pear trees that fruited poorly, and a pond kept clean by a basic formation.
Leon found Loriel forty minutes later, sitting on her heels with both palms against the soil.

"The drainage is wrong," she said without looking up. "There’s a spiritual vein beneath the eastern corner, but everything was planted on the western side where the ground remains cold. Whoever planned this worked from a diagram and never touched the soil."
She sat back and looked around.
"It’s mine now. Tell someone."
"It’s yours."
"Good." Loriel studied the eastern corner. "The fern goes there eventually. Not yet."
"How long?"

"Months." She said it without disappointment. "It has spent too long inside a vessel filled with soil from another world. If I plant it directly in Jade Moon soil, it may shock, die, or root badly enough that it never produces seeds."
"What will you do?"
"A little of its original soil goes into the new bed. Then some of the new soil goes into its current vessel. I repeat the exchange until the plant stops noticing the difference."
"And if it notices?"
"Then I lose several months, and the fern remains alive." Loriel looked up. "That is the point of doing it slowly."
Seraphine waited until the residence became busy before finding Leon.
"Sit down," she said.
Leon sat.
"Your cultivation route."
"It’s mostly recovered."

"That is the second time you’ve used ’mostly’ about something inside your own body." Seraphine took the seat opposite him. "So I’ll ask precisely. Is the route restored, or has it merely stopped worsening?"
Leon considered lying and discarded the idea almost immediately.

"The tears have closed. The junctions hold ordinary circulation, and I’ve run it clean every day for more than a week." He turned his cup between his fingers. "There’s still stiffness in the lower-left route when I force a high volume through it. Ji believes it will fade if I leave it alone."
"Thank you."
Seraphine allowed a short pause.
"Now the other matter. You won."
"I did."
"Tell me why."
He did, because she had earned the honest version and because saying it aloud was useful.

"Wei began under Peak Golden Core suppression, which removed most of what made him a Mid Void Immortal. His technique was unfinished. Once it took hold, it trapped him inside the same repeating lunar pattern."
Leon shook his head.

"After the suppression broke, he was fighting the technique as much as he was fighting me. His judgment deteriorated with his control. The duel also lasted twenty minutes. I don’t tire the way ordinary cultivators do. Every minute after the first ten favored me more than him."
"And if he had been clear-headed?" Seraphine asked. "Full cultivation, with proper control?"

"I don’t know." Leon met her gaze. "A Mid Void Immortal who changes his pattern when I begin reading it would force me to reveal far more than I did. Even then, I might lose. What happened in that arena isn’t something I can reproduce whenever I choose."
Seraphine released a quiet breath.
"That’s all I wanted."
"Not for me to be careful?"
"For you to understand the difference between winning and being stronger—and to tell me instead of deciding I would worry too much to hear it."
"Understood."
"Good."
Seraphine stood. As she passed, she rested a hand on his shoulder for a moment.
"The eastern wall seam is genuinely bad," she added. "I’m reporting it to Han Suwen tomorrow through the proper channel, like a well-behaved attendant."
That evening, Leon sat in the main hall with the doors open and did no work at all.

Vyra’s voice carried from the delivery court as she informed someone that both access tokens would be entered into the ledger by morning. Ira came up the path complaining about a disciple’s back foot. Loriel was asking a bewildered gardener whether the Palace kept river sand. Seraphine walked the inner boundary twice, confirming that no servant had crossed it.
A month earlier, the residence had been quiet enough for Leon to hear the leaves shifting on the plum tree.
He listened to the women filling that silence and found he did not miss it.

Two disciples were sparring with practice spears.
Ira’s head turned and remained turned for the next eleven paces.
"You seem deeply unimpressed," Vyra said.
"Their footwork is wrong."
"Mm."
"It is.
The taller one plants his rear foot before committing, so the thrust can be read half a beat early." Ira faced forward.
"I was judging their form.
Professionally."
"Of course."
Leon’s residence had a staff of nine responsible for the outer paths, delivery court, kitchens, guest rooms, and grounds beyond the inner wall.
They had spent the past month maintaining a residence for one man who was rarely in the building.
Now they lined up in the front courtyard and bowed, visibly uncertain what to do with four additional household members.
The inner grounds operated differently.
Leon’s cultivation chambers remained sealed.
The women’s quarters stood inside the protected boundary, and no outside staff member could enter without permission.
Anything connected to the dimensional world, their Classes, or Leon’s deeper secrets would be discussed only inside those wards.
Vyra requested the staff list, supply records, access tokens, maintenance schedule, and household inventory within twenty minutes.
She found no corruption or sabotage.
The residence had simply been established for one secluded disciple and had never been updated for anything else.
"There are two delivery-court tokens, and neither is listed in the residence ledger," she said.
"The kitchen orders food for one person but has over-ordered rice for three weeks because nobody corrected the standing request.
The eastern wall is inspected quarterly despite being the most recently repaired section."
She turned another page.
"The repair was handled by the same crew responsible for the seam Seraphine noticed at the harbor."
"Can you fix it?" Leon asked.
"Most of it within a week." Vyra continued reading.
"Ira."
Ira had left two of her three bags beside the entrance and was already moving toward the door.
"I’m going to inspect the western platform."
"We have been inside this residence for eleven minutes."
"Plenty of time to inspect a platform."
"You left your luggage in the middle of a walkway.
A servant moves it, a servant handles a combat guard’s equipment, and tomorrow I spend an hour explaining to Seraphine why an unvetted person touched your belongings." Vyra raised her eyes.
"Take the bags."
Ira collected them, grumbling all the way to her quarters.
She returned three minutes later and left for the platform anyway.
Nobody stopped her.
Loriel discovered the inner garden and disappeared into it.
It was not ruined.

It had been planted competently decades ago with species chosen almost entirely because they survived neglect: silver-thorn along the walls, two moon-pear trees that fruited poorly, and a pond kept clean by a basic formation.
Leon found Loriel forty minutes later, sitting on her heels with both palms against the soil.
"The drainage is wrong," she said without looking up.
"There’s a spiritual vein beneath the eastern corner, but everything was planted on the western side where the ground remains cold.
Whoever planned this worked from a diagram and never touched the soil."
She sat back and looked around.
"It’s mine now.
Tell someone."
"It’s yours."
"Good." Loriel studied the eastern corner.
"The fern goes there eventually.
Not yet."
"How long?"
"Months." She said it without disappointment.
"It has spent too long inside a vessel filled with soil from another world.
If I plant it directly in Jade Moon soil, it may shock, die, or root badly enough that it never produces seeds."
"What will you do?"
"A little of its original soil goes into the new bed.
Then some of the new soil goes into its current vessel.
I repeat the exchange until the plant stops noticing the difference."
"And if it notices?"
"Then I lose several months, and the fern remains alive." Loriel looked up.
"That is the point of doing it slowly."
Seraphine waited until the residence became busy before finding Leon.
"Sit down," she said.
Leon sat.
"Your cultivation route."
"It’s mostly recovered."
"That is the second time you’ve used ’mostly’ about something inside your own body." Seraphine took the seat opposite him.
"So I’ll ask precisely.
Is the route restored, or has it merely stopped worsening?"
Leon considered lying and discarded the idea almost immediately.
"The tears have closed.
The junctions hold ordinary circulation, and I’ve run it clean every day for more than a week." He turned his cup between his fingers.
"There’s still stiffness in the lower-left route when I force a high volume through it.
Ji believes it will fade if I leave it alone."
"Thank you."
Seraphine allowed a short pause.
"Now the other matter.
You won."
"I did."
"Tell me why."
He did, because she had earned the honest version and because saying it aloud was useful.
"Wei began under Peak Golden Core suppression, which removed most of what made him a Mid Void Immortal.
His technique was unfinished.
Once it took hold, it trapped him inside the same repeating lunar pattern."
Leon shook his head.
"After the suppression broke, he was fighting the technique as much as he was fighting me.
His judgment deteriorated with his control.
The duel also lasted twenty minutes.
I don’t tire the way ordinary cultivators do.
Every minute after the first ten favored me more than him."
"And if he had been clear-headed?" Seraphine asked.
"Full cultivation, with proper control?"
"I don’t know." Leon met her gaze.
"A Mid Void Immortal who changes his pattern when I begin reading it would force me to reveal far more than I did.
Even then, I might lose.
What happened in that arena isn’t something I can reproduce whenever I choose."
Seraphine released a quiet breath.
"That’s all I wanted."
"Not for me to be careful?"
"For you to understand the difference between winning and being stronger—and to tell me instead of deciding I would worry too much to hear it."
"Understood."
"Good."
Seraphine stood.
As she passed, she rested a hand on his shoulder for a moment.
"The eastern wall seam is genuinely bad," she added.
"I’m reporting it to Han Suwen tomorrow through the proper channel, like a well-behaved attendant."
That evening, Leon sat in the main hall with the doors open and did no work at all.
Vyra’s voice carried from the delivery court as she informed someone that both access tokens would be entered into the ledger by morning.
Ira came up the path complaining about a disciple’s back foot.
Loriel was asking a bewildered gardener whether the Palace kept river sand.
Seraphine walked the inner boundary twice, confirming that no servant had crossed it.
A month earlier, the residence had been quiet enough for Leon to hear the leaves shifting on the plum tree.
He listened to the women filling that silence and found he did not miss it.

chapters.title: Chapter 638: The Palace Mistress at the Door
paragraphs: Han Suwen returned on the first morning and remained for two hours.
By the time she left, she and Vyra had established the entire administrative structure of the household.

They sat at the long table in the outer hall with three ledgers open between them. They discussed the monthly allowance, how it was drawn, and how requesting materials instead of spirit stones could provide better value if the order was submitted a week in advance.

Han Suwen opened separate contribution accounts for each attendant, although all four currently held nothing. Vyra narrowed the permissions granted to the outer staff. Repairs went through the formation hall, missions through outer administration, and household attendants could access the general foundational library but nothing restricted.
"The missing delivery token," Vyra said near the end.

"I found it." Han Suwen produced a record slip. "A maintenance crew received it during the second week and returned it correctly, but the notice confirming its return was sent to a disciple in seclusion."
"So the fault is in the notification route."

"The fault is that Jade Moon Palace has four hundred residences and assumes someone reads every message sent to them." Han Suwen closed her ledger. "You will find more errors like it. Send them to me, and I will correct the ones within my authority."
They did not become friends. They resolved a month’s worth of administrative problems in two hours and parted with a mutual recognition of competence, which was enough for both of them.
Over the next two days, Leon found himself drawn into everyone else’s projects.

Seraphine walked him through the residence’s defenses on the first afternoon. Two of its six arrays were self-contained. Three depended upon scheduled maintenance from the formation hall and would begin degrading if those rotations stopped. The sixth, hidden beneath the main hall, was Ji Liansu’s work.
Seraphine had spent an hour studying what little of its structure she could perceive and had come away impressed and irritated.
"If the Palace ever wanted to restrict this residence, it wouldn’t need to attack," she said. "Stopping three maintenance rotations would weaken most of the outer protection within a season."
"Is that a warning?"
"It’s a fact I want both of us to remember."
Ira returned from the western platform on the second day in a foul mood.

She had spent four hours there and defeated two Foundation Establishment disciples without revealing anything unusual. An Early Golden Core disciple had then offered her a match, apparently expecting an amusing afternoon against a household attendant.
Ira had declined.
"I could have beaten him," she said, dropping onto a bench.
"Probably."
"Probably?" She glared at Leon. "Definitely. His stance was—"
She stopped.

"It doesn’t matter. If I defeat an Early Golden Core disciple in front of thirty witnesses on my second day, people begin asking why a Peak Foundation attendant can do it. Then someone who understands what they’re seeing comes to watch the next match."
"That’s the correct conclusion."
"I know it’s correct. I hate it." Ira stretched her arms above her head. "Eventually, I’m going to have to lose one deliberately."
"That would be convincing."
"I’d rather be stabbed."

Loriel had the eastern corner of the garden turned over by the end of the second day. She had begun exchanging the fern’s soil a double handful at a time and written a schedule on a board that only she seemed able to understand.
Ji Liansu arrived on the third morning without an announcement.
Leon sensed her a fraction before anyone else. The outer staff fell silent in the delivery court. Han Suwen, who had come up with a supply notice, straightened and moved aside.
The residence formations did not react at all. They recognized their maker and allowed her through.
Ji walked up the path alone, dressed in pale green and silver-grey, her veil covering the lower half of her face.
The four women were already waiting in the courtyard when Leon reached the door. Vyra had arranged them properly without being told.
They bowed.
Ji allowed the gesture, then motioned for them to rise.
"You are Leon’s household," she said. "You are not his possessions, and you are not mine. I want that understood now rather than assumed later."
"Palace Mistress," Vyra acknowledged.

"You are under his protection, which places you under mine as well. Both are real. If a disciple or official attempts to exploit your status as attendants, report it. Jade Moon Palace will address it through its authority rather than allowing private retaliation."
Her gaze moved across them.

"It also means your conduct reflects upon Leon. He is my direct disciple, and there are people on this mountain who would welcome a reason to say that accepting him was a mistake. Do not provide one."
"Understood," Seraphine said.
Ji studied the four women without releasing a probe or pushing spiritual pressure into their foundations. Her attention remained calm and unhurried.

"Your foundations are more stable than those of any Peak Foundation Establishment cultivator I’ve examined in the past decade," she said. "Your control exceeds your recorded realm, and all four of you move like people with considerable combat experience."
Nobody answered. It had not been a question.
"Your inheritance is your own," Ji continued. "I have one recommendation. Do not rush Golden Core."
She stepped closer to Loriel and examined the faint soil beneath her fingernails before returning her attention to the group.

"All four of you reached this point at a speed I do not fully understand. That does not mean you should decide the next breakthrough by a calendar. Consolidate your foundations. Learn how your new circulation responds under different conditions. Study how Golden Core condensation is practised here before assuming manuals have taught you everything. Most importantly, find materials compatible with your individual paths rather than accepting whatever is easiest to purchase."
"How long would you recommend?" Vyra asked.

"For an ordinary Peak Foundation cultivator with good resources? Years." Ji tilted her head. "For the four of you, a number would be misleading. Break through when your foundations, comprehension, and materials are ready—not when impatience chooses a date."
Ji spoke with Leon alone afterward as they walked along the inner path.
"Your cultivation route?" she asked.
"Clean circulation for more than a week. Some stiffness when I push too much volume through the lower-left junction."
"Then continue what you’re doing and attempt nothing clever. You will not touch the second stage until the stiffness is gone and your channels remain stable under full circulation."
"I wasn’t planning to."
"That answer would reassure me more if I hadn’t watched you invent the first stage."
Ji stopped beside the plum tree.
"The garden has been dug up."
"Loriel claimed it."
"Mm."
She looked toward the turned soil in the eastern corner.
"You are talking more."
"Am I?"
"You answered four questions this morning without first deciding what each answer might cost you. You haven’t done that since arriving here."
Ji resumed walking.
"I approve. A disciple with nobody around whom he can relax eventually chooses the wrong place to become careless."
That was all she said about it.
Han Suwen waited at the gate after Ji departed, holding a folded notice bearing a seal Leon did not recognize.

"This arrived an hour ago. I held it until the Palace Mistress had finished her visit." She offered it to him. "Supreme Elder Wei Shouyuan requests permission to visit this residence. He will be accompanied by Wei Zhaoran."
Vyra took the notice, read it, and passed it to Leon.
"Is Wei coming to apologize," Ira asked, "or to request another beating?"
"Neither," Vyra said. "A Peak Earth Immortal does not request permission to visit a Golden Core disciple’s residence unless he intends to settle something formally."
Ira’s eyebrows rose.
"Peak Earth Immortal."
"Which is why," Seraphine said, "you will stand somewhere quiet and refrain from speaking."

chapters.title: Chapter 639: A Debt Cut in Jade
paragraphs: Wei Shouyuan and Wei Zhaoran arrived later that afternoon.
They came on foot up the mountain path like ordinary visitors.

Leon sensed Wei Shouyuan from a considerable distance, but the old man’s cultivation quickly passed beyond anything he could measure. No spiritual pressure rolled ahead of him. The nearby formations remained undisturbed, and the birds in the plum plum tree continued calling.
He isn’t here to test me.

Vyra received them at the gate with the proper etiquette. Leon waited in the outer hall and greeted Wei Shouyuan as a powerful senior without descending the steps to meet him. As Ji Liansu’s direct disciple, lowering himself too far would disrespect his master’s position.
Wei Shouyuan was tall, with a weathered face and a posture that age had done nothing to weaken. A sword hung at his side.
His gaze travelled once around the hall, taking in the four women and where each had positioned herself, before returning to Leon.
Wei Zhaoran entered behind him and remained standing.
"Say it," Wei Shouyuan ordered.
Wei Zhaoran was silent for several breaths.

"I brought a technique into a supervised duel that I had not finished learning," he said at last. His voice was flat and careful, and he did not initially meet Leon’s eyes. "I knew it was unfinished. I had been warned not to use it under suppression, and I agreed."
His hands tightened once at his sides.
"When I invoked it, I already understood that I was losing. I told myself I could keep it within the limit."
He stopped, then forced himself to continue.
"Two exchanges later, I knew my control was failing. I continued anyway. That is the part I have not been able to excuse."
Wei finally looked at Leon.
"The suppression breaking was not the first failure. The first failure was feeling the technique slip and refusing to stop because stopping meant conceding in front of three hundred witnesses."
"And afterward?" Wei Shouyuan asked.
"Afterward, I lost the domain entirely. I was no longer in command of myself, and I cannot claim to know what I intended because I was no longer capable of proper intent."
Wei’s jaw tightened.

"You had already won. Everyone on the terrace watched you force me back before I invoked the false moon, and I will not allow anyone from my line to describe the result differently. When the backlash began, you could have withdrawn. My channels were opening. Another twenty seconds would have damaged my foundation beyond recovery."
He bowed deeply.

"You held the technique together instead. I have seen the record of what doing so inflicted upon your own cultivation route. I possess nothing that would balance that choice. I can only acknowledge it plainly."
Leon allowed the silence to remain long enough for the apology to settle.
"Thank you," he said. "I accept it. And neither of us is going to repeat what happened."
"Then—"
"But I want to correct one thing."
Leon leaned back slightly.

"You’ve had nearly a month to rebuild that duel into something worse than it was. You suppressed yourself to Peak Golden Core. That stripped away most of what made you a Mid Void Immortal. Your unfinished technique trapped you in a repeating pattern, and I found the seams in that pattern."
Wei listened without interrupting.
"I didn’t overpower the full technique. I unpicked it because you had stopped changing what you were doing. The duel also continued for twenty minutes. That favors me more than almost anyone alive."
Wei remained still.

"A clear-headed Mid Void Immortal using his full cultivation and adapting when I begin reading him is a different opponent," Leon continued. "I don’t know how that fight ends. I would have to reveal considerably more than I did, and I might still lose. What happened in the arena isn’t something I can reproduce on command."
Some of the strain left Wei’s expression.
"You could have allowed me to believe otherwise."
"It wouldn’t have been true. You would eventually have learned that in a worse way."
Wei took a measured breath.
"Then I want a second match."
"Not now," Leon said.

"No. Not now." For the first time, Wei’s voice held something resembling its old certainty. "When I’ve mastered what I claimed to understand, and when you’ve progressed as far as you are clearly intending to go."
His gaze hardened.
"A clean match. No suppression. No unfinished techniques. Nobody carrying the other man out afterward."
"Agreed."
"Good." Wei hesitated. "I was told your recovery was not brief."
"It wasn’t."
"Then I’m glad you are standing."
Wei Shouyuan had allowed the exchange to proceed without interruption. He now set his cup down.
"His discipline has been handled," he said. "It was severe, it was mine to administer, and it is complete. I did not come here to ask you to soften the truth for him. I’m pleased that you did not."
"He would have known."
"He would."
Wei Shouyuan studied Leon.
"The debt is separate from the discipline. My descendant’s foundation remains intact because a man he challenged, wounded, and endangered chose to preserve it. I will not leave that unpaid."
He drew a pale jade rectangle from his sleeve and placed it on the table. It was the length of Leon’s thumb, with one character carved into its face and a narrow line of script along its edge.
"A personal warrant," Wei Shouyuan said. "Mine, not my lineage’s."
Leon examined it without reaching for it.
"Explain it to me. I would rather ask now than assume."
"Sensible."
Wei Shouyuan turned the jade so Leon could see the inscription.
"It records one favor owed by me personally. Whoever holds it may present it, state what they require, and I will fulfill the request. Once used, the warrant is spent and the debt is closed."
"Limits?"

"Three, and they are absolute. It cannot compel me to act against Jade Moon Palace. It cannot override sect law. If you ask me to free someone the Palace has properly condemned, I will refuse and the warrant will remain unspent."
He touched the final line of script.

"It also cannot require any action that threatens the Palace’s survival. Within those limits, I will not argue over whether your request is important enough. If you spend it on something small, that is your choice."
Leon lifted the warrant. It weighed almost nothing.
Refusing would not be humility. A properly acknowledged life-debt from a Supreme Elder could not be dismissed without insulting the integrity of the man offering it.
"Thank you," Leon said. "I’ll try not to waste it."
"Waste it if you need to. That is what it is for."
The visitors remained for another quarter hour, speaking of less important matters, before departing.
Once the gate closed behind them, the tension throughout the residence eased.
Vyra had the warrant in her hands within a minute.
"This is worth more than a vault," she said. "A Peak Earth Immortal, obligated once, at a time of our choosing. There is no single treasure in this Palace I would trade it for."
She turned it over carefully.
"It needs a secure location. Not a drawer. Somewhere that survives the residence burning down."
"You’ll find one."
"I’ll find three." Vyra paused. "Nobody outside this room should learn we possess it. Its usefulness decreases the moment other factions begin planning around it."
Ira folded her arms.
"So you’re actually going to fight Wei again."
"Eventually."
"After spending more than a week testing a damaged cultivation route."
"That’s why I said eventually."
"Hm."
She did not appear convinced, but she allowed the matter to end.

Seraphine said nothing. She had known Leon’s answer before Wei finished making the request. From her expression, she had already begun considering how powerful both men might be when that rematch arrived.
Loriel spoke last. She stood in the doorway with a trowel still in one hand.
"Whenever it happens," she said, "could you arrange to return without any part of you being described as mostly healed? I’ve heard that phrase twice now, and I dislike it."
"I’ll do my best."
"That is what you said last time."
The summons arrived the following morning, three full days after the women entered Jade Moon Palace.
Han Suwen delivered it personally. That was the first indication that it mattered.
The message was sealed. That was the second.
It named all five of them.
Leon. Seraphine. Ira. Vyra. Loriel. Private briefing chamber, fourth mark, today.
Leon read it twice.
His master normally summoned a disciple. If she needed something from the disciple’s household, she expected the disciple to arrange it.
Naming all four attendants meant Ji intended them to hear the same information at the same time.
So this isn’t an errand.

Wei finally looked at Leon.
"The suppression breaking was not the first failure.
The first failure was feeling the technique slip and refusing to stop because stopping meant conceding in front of three hundred witnesses."
"And afterward?" Wei Shouyuan asked.
"Afterward, I lost the domain entirely.
I was no longer in command of myself, and I cannot claim to know what I intended because I was no longer capable of proper intent."
Wei’s jaw tightened.
"You had already won.
Everyone on the terrace watched you force me back before I invoked the false moon, and I will not allow anyone from my line to describe the result differently.
When the backlash began, you could have withdrawn.
My channels were opening.
Another twenty seconds would have damaged my foundation beyond recovery."
He bowed deeply.
"You held the technique together instead.
I have seen the record of what doing so inflicted upon your own cultivation route.
I possess nothing that would balance that choice.
I can only acknowledge it plainly."
Leon allowed the silence to remain long enough for the apology to settle.
"Thank you," he said.
"I accept it.
And neither of us is going to repeat what happened."
"Then—"
"But I want to correct one thing."
Leon leaned back slightly.
"You’ve had nearly a month to rebuild that duel into something worse than it was.
You suppressed yourself to Peak Golden Core.
That stripped away most of what made you a Mid Void Immortal.
Your unfinished technique trapped you in a repeating pattern, and I found the seams in that pattern."
Wei listened without interrupting.
"I didn’t overpower the full technique.
I unpicked it because you had stopped changing what you were doing.
The duel also continued for twenty minutes.
That favors me more than almost anyone alive."
Wei remained still.
"A clear-headed Mid Void Immortal using his full cultivation and adapting when I begin reading him is a different opponent," Leon continued.
"I don’t know how that fight ends.
I would have to reveal considerably more than I did, and I might still lose.
What happened in the arena isn’t something I can reproduce on command."
Some of the strain left Wei’s expression.
"You could have allowed me to believe otherwise."
"It wouldn’t have been true.
You would eventually have learned that in a worse way."
Wei took a measured breath.
"Then I want a second match."
"Not now," Leon said.
"No.
Not now." For the first time, Wei’s voice held something resembling its old certainty.
"When I’ve mastered what I claimed to understand, and when you’ve progressed as far as you are clearly intending to go."
His gaze hardened.
"A clean match.
No suppression.
No unfinished techniques.
Nobody carrying the other man out afterward."
"Agreed."
"Good." Wei hesitated.
"I was told your recovery was not brief."
"It wasn’t."
"Then I’m glad you are standing."
Wei Shouyuan had allowed the exchange to proceed without interruption.
He now set his cup down.
"His discipline has been handled," he said.
"It was severe, it was mine to administer, and it is complete.
I did not come here to ask you to soften the truth for him.
I’m pleased that you did not."
"He would have known."
"He would."
Wei Shouyuan studied Leon.
"The debt is separate from the discipline.
My descendant’s foundation remains intact because a man he challenged, wounded, and endangered chose to preserve it.
I will not leave that unpaid."
He drew a pale jade rectangle from his sleeve and placed it on the table.
It was the length of Leon’s thumb, with one character carved into its face and a narrow line of script along its edge.
"A personal warrant," Wei Shouyuan said.
"Mine, not my lineage’s."
Leon examined it without reaching for it.
"Explain it to me.
I would rather ask now than assume."
"Sensible."
Wei Shouyuan turned the jade so Leon could see the inscription.
"It records one favor owed by me personally.
Whoever holds it may present it, state what they require, and I will fulfill the request.
Once used, the warrant is spent and the debt is closed."
"Limits?"
"Three, and they are absolute.
It cannot compel me to act against Jade Moon Palace.
It cannot override sect law.
If you ask me to free someone the Palace has properly condemned, I will refuse and the warrant will remain unspent."
He touched the final line of script.
"It also cannot require any action that threatens the Palace’s survival.
Within those limits, I will not argue over whether your request is important enough.
If you spend it on something small, that is your choice."
Leon lifted the warrant.
It weighed almost nothing.
Refusing would not be humility.
A properly acknowledged life-debt from a Supreme Elder could not be dismissed without insulting the integrity of the man offering it.
"Thank you," Leon said.
"I’ll try not to waste it."
"Waste it if you need to.
That is what it is for."
The visitors remained for another quarter hour, speaking of less important matters, before departing.
Once the gate closed behind them, the tension throughout the residence eased.
Vyra had the warrant in her hands within a minute.
"This is worth more than a vault," she said.
"A Peak Earth Immortal, obligated once, at a time of our choosing.
There is no single treasure in this Palace I would trade it for."
She turned it over carefully.
"It needs a secure location.
Not a drawer.
Somewhere that survives the residence burning down."
"You’ll find one."
"I’ll find three." Vyra paused.
"Nobody outside this room should learn we possess it.
Its usefulness decreases the moment other factions begin planning around it."
Ira folded her arms.
"So you’re actually going to fight Wei again."
"Eventually."
"After spending more than a week testing a damaged cultivation route."
"That’s why I said eventually."
"Hm."
She did not appear convinced, but she allowed the matter to end.
Seraphine said nothing.
She had known Leon’s answer before Wei finished making the request.
From her expression, she had already begun considering how powerful both men might be when that rematch arrived.
Loriel spoke last.
She stood in the doorway with a trowel still in one hand.
"Whenever it happens," she said, "could you arrange to return without any part of you being described as mostly healed?
I’ve heard that phrase twice now, and I dislike it."
"I’ll do my best."
"That is what you said last time."
The summons arrived the following morning, three full days after the women entered Jade Moon Palace.
Han Suwen delivered it personally.
That was the first indication that it mattered.
The message was sealed.
That was the second.
It named all five of them.
Leon.
Seraphine.
Ira.
Vyra.
Loriel.
Private briefing chamber, fourth mark, today.
Leon read it twice.
His master normally summoned a disciple.
If she needed something from the disciple’s household, she expected the disciple to arrange it.
Naming all four attendants meant Ji intended them to hear the same information at the same time.
So this isn’t an errand.

chapters.title: Chapter 640: When Rain Climbs to Heaven
paragraphs: The briefing chamber was small, windowless, and protected by an isolation array considerably better than anything Leon could currently build.
Ji Liansu was already waiting. Han Suwen sat at a side table beside a case of records, a folded map, and three sealed jars.
"Sit," Ji said. "All of you."
She waited until they had taken their places.

"This is an offer, not an order. Your household has existed publicly for three days. If you refuse, there will be no penalty, no mark against you, and no loss of favor. I will offer the assignment to another team."
Ji unrolled the map.
It showed a rough oval nearly sixty kilometers across. The outer regions were recorded in detail, while the center contained large stretches of unfinished terrain.

"Ashen Rain Basin," Ji said. "It lies eleven days away along the northern route, inside territory monitored by Jade Moon Palace. The basin is an impact region. Something struck the continent there a very long time ago, and its geology never fully settled."
Han Suwen placed the first sample jar on the table.
Inside rested a dark glasslike shard crossed by pale branching lines.

"Stormglass," Ji said. "Lightning strikes that basin more frequently than anywhere else on this continent. Where ancient strikes met impact-heated mineral, the two fused. Stormglass holds a charge for an extremely long time and is difficult to refine."
Seraphine leaned forward slightly but said nothing.
The second jar contained grey ore threaded with red.
"Flame vents run beneath the eastern basin. Ore taken from the surrounding rock accepts fire-aligned energy easily. Deeper crystals have been found, but never in enough quantity for proper study."
Ira and Vyra examined the same sample with entirely different expressions.
The third jar contained a thick-stemmed cutting suspended in preservative. A faint glow pulsed beneath its outer layer.
"Mineral springs, heated soil, and unusual ambient energy produce aggressive medicinal growth," Ji continued. "Some species appear nowhere else."
Loriel went still.

"Understand what these are," Ji said. "Raw materials from a dangerous region. None is a finished treasure, and none will grant an effortless breakthrough. After evaluation and refinement, however, they may suit your individual foundations better than whatever the medicine court keeps in ordinary stock."
"That is an honest way to present it," Vyra said.
"I would prefer that you accept for the correct reason—or refuse for one."
Ji turned the map over.
"Now the part that matters."
A route had been drawn across the western side of the basin. Nine markers followed it before stopping abruptly.

"Nine days ago, a survey team ceased reporting. One Late Golden Core deacon, two Early Golden Core disciples, and six Foundation Establishment surveyors. Their assignment was to verify a newly exposed resource region and update the western map."
"No distress signal?" Seraphine asked.
"None. They failed to report at their scheduled daily window and have missed every window since." Ji rested one finger against the final marker. "All nine life tablets remain intact."
Ira leaned forward.
"So they’re alive."

"Their life imprints have not been severed," Ji corrected. "That is what the tablets prove. They may be alive and unable to signal. They may be imprisoned. They may be caught in a condition that has not broken the imprint. Do not claim more than the evidence supports."
"And no team entered after them?" Vyra asked.

"Two Nascent Soul patrols swept the perimeter and tested the outer routes. They found no immortal-level presence, no trace of a large engagement, and no evidence of the basin’s ordinary formations collapsing."
Ji indicated several notes along the basin’s edge.
"No terrain was displaced. No battle residue was found. Nothing outside the missing team’s final survey region indicates that nine people disappeared there."
"Why not send one of those patrols inside?" Leon asked.
"Under ordinary circumstances, I would."
Ji met his gaze.

"I’m offering the assignment to you because you have demonstrated spatial mobility, the ability to survive an unstable domain, and combat strength beyond that of an ordinary Golden Core cultivator. Your household also contains security, combat, formation, and medicinal expertise in a small group."
She folded her hands on the table.

"You are not less valuable than a Nascent Soul patrol, and you are not being sent because you are expendable. You are being considered because your group is better suited to enter quietly, investigate, and withdraw without announcing to every faction watching our northern territory that Jade Moon Palace may have discovered something serious."
"A spatial fold?" Leon asked.

"Possibly. A damaged formation is another possibility. So is an unknown resource affecting the tracking arrays." Ji paused. "Those are theories. We do not yet possess enough evidence to choose among them."
Han Suwen read the safeguards from her list.

Five single-use emergency return talismans, each anchored to a receiving array inside Jade Moon Palace. Fixed communication windows every second day. Updated maps, complete around the basin’s edge and clearly marked where information became unreliable. The missing team’s planned route and record-formation frequencies.
They also had standing authority to retreat.
"If the danger exceeds the assigned classification, you withdraw," Ji said. "You do not remain to verify it. You do not seek additional proof. You return and report."
Her gaze moved across all five of them.
"If you miss a communication window, a stronger response will depart within the hour, whether you want it or not."
"What are the objectives?" Vyra asked, already writing.
Ji listed them.

"Verify the newly exposed resource region. Locate and recover the missing team’s record plaques. Determine why the tracking formations failed. Find and extract the survey team if it can be done safely."
She paused before the last.
"If you confirm an immortal-level danger, withdraw and report. That instruction is not last in importance."
Their roles emerged during the questions that followed.

Seraphine took route security and detection after asking about the patrols’ sweep patterns. Ira would respond when something required direct force. Vyra claimed supplies, communication schedules, record formations, and route management. Loriel would examine the local growth, life traces, injuries, and signs of environmental corruption.
Leon would lead and decide when the group turned back.
"There is one more record," Ji said. "It is the reason this briefing is taking place inside a sealed chamber."
She placed a small plaque on the table and touched its surface.
A grainy projection appeared above it.
Rain fell over dark stone and sparse, hard-leaved trees. Steam rose from cracks in three places. A line of survey markers stretched toward a distant ridge.
A middle-aged man in deacon-grey stood with his back partly toward the recorder, giving routine instructions about marker spacing.
The scene was wet, cold, and unremarkable.
A bead of water trembled on a leaf near the edge of the projection.
Instead of falling, it detached from the leaf and rose in a straight line.
"There," Loriel said quietly.
More droplets followed.
Water lifted from puddles between the stones. At first, it rose in loose drops. Then the droplets joined into narrow silver streams climbing from the ground toward the clouds.
Ordinary rain continued falling. The descending water passed through the rising streams without either changing direction.
One of the surveyors shouted something indistinct.
The deacon turned.
Three members of the team activated tracking formations.
Every needle swung at the same moment.
They did not point toward the Palace route. They did not indicate the survey markers, the deacon, or any of the nine cultivators standing in the clearing.
All three settled upon the same bearing.
Their points aimed toward a stretch of flat, apparently empty ground at the edge of the projection.
"Same bearing on all three," Vyra murmured.
The image distorted around the edges. Water continued rising while the deacon began to speak.
The recording faded before his words became clear.
It ended without a cry, an impact, or any visible attacker.
Ji closed her hand, extinguishing the projection.

"The needles may have been redirected," Vyra said into the quiet. "A damaged tracking formation usually produces inconsistent movement, locks onto an old signal, or fails to settle. Three separate formations agreeing that precisely suggests they were still detecting something."

"Or being made to believe they were," Seraphine said. She looked at the empty space where the projection had been. "Either way, that ground is our strongest lead. It is not yet proof of what happened."
Loriel had not moved.
"The leaves remained in place," she said. "Only the water moved. Whatever caused it was not pulling everything equally, and it began before the surveyors activated their formations."

"A draw rather than an attack," Ira said. Her arms were folded, and for once there was no grin on her face. "Maybe. Nine cultivators disappeared without enough warning for one of them to trigger a distress signal. That’s the part I dislike."
Leon studied the map.
Eleven days away. Nine cultivators whose life tablets remained intact. Materials suited to every member of his household. A Palace response waiting if they missed a scheduled report.
And an empty stretch of ground that three tracking formations had identified while rain climbed toward the sky.
Leon looked at Ji Liansu.
"When do we leave?"

chapters.title: Chapter 641: Eleven Days North
paragraphs: "Tomorrow morning," said Ji Liansu.

She was already rolling the map. "You have tonight to prepare, which is less than you want and more than the survey team has. One thing before you go, and I am not going to repeat the rest of the briefing."
She looked at each of them in turn.

"If you confirm an immortal-level danger, you leave. If you reach a point where you cannot reliably judge what you are facing, you also leave. Either condition is enough." Her eyes settled on Leon last. "You do not remain to verify your conclusion, and you do not stay because retreat would look poor in a report. Pride has killed more capable people in that basin than lightning has."
"Understood."
Han Suwen laid the equipment out on the table.

Five talismans first, each a folded strip of stiff paper with a jade thread through it, sealed and heavier than paper had any business being. "Single use. Anchored to a receiving array under the eastern terrace. Tear it and you arrive there, wherever you are and whatever is holding you, unless something is actively suppressing space in a way I have never personally seen."
Leon took all five, and then handed them out himself.
He passed one to each woman and watched until all four had secured theirs in separate places.
Vyra raised an eyebrow. "I could carry them."
"No."
"They’d be organized."

"They’d be in one place," Leon said, "and if that place is separated from the rest of us, four people have no way home." He tucked the last into his own collar. "Everyone carries their own. Every day. Even in camp."
Vyra accepted that without argument and made a note.

The rest followed: the communication plaques, keyed to windows every second day at the third and eleventh marks. The survey team’s route records and the frequencies their formations had been running. A map that was excellent for forty kilometers and then showed a blank oval with a hand-inked line around it and the wordsincomplete surveywritten twice. Sample containers, sealed cases, field supplies.
"Miss a window," Han Suwen said, "and a response leaves within the hour. That is automatic. Nobody has to decide it."
They spent the evening preparing, and Leon watched his household turn into a field unit without giving a single instruction.

Vyra had the provisions counted twice and the equipment distributed by weight before the second mark, and then went through the contingencies aloud — what happened if the plaques failed, what happened if they were separated, which of them carried the spare sample seals, and where the reserve stones sat.

Seraphine took the route records and the map to the far end of the table and stayed there for two hours. When she came back she had a watch order, three rest points chosen for sight lines rather than comfort, and an opinion about how they should move if the storms came in.

"Poor visibility, we go in a stretched diamond," she said. "Ira forward and left, me forward and right, Leon center, Loriel behind Leon, Vyra rear. Nobody more than eight paces from two other people. If we lose sight of each other, everybody stops. No searching."
"Agreed," said Leon.
Loriel had commandeered a side table and was choosing containers, which turned out to be a considerably longer job than choosing medicines.

"Sealed jade for anything with an active vitality signature," she said, mostly to herself. "Wood for the dry material. Nothing in the copper cases — copper leeches. And I want three empty containers that have never held anything at all, because if there’s something in that basin nobody’s catalogued, I’m not putting it in a jar that spent four years holding blood-lotus."
Ira had been ready in twenty minutes and had spent the two hours since being visibly ready.
"We’re going to a wasteland to look for nine people," she said, on the third pass through Vyra’s contingency list. "How many ways are there to carry rope."
"Four," said Vyra, without looking up. "One of which you have chosen, and it is the wrong one, because you have coiled it so it will snag."
"It won’t snag."
"It will snag, and it will snag at the exact moment somebody is hanging from it." Vyra held out a hand. "Give it here."
Ira gave it over, made a noise of protest that lasted approximately one second, and then leaned over to watch how Vyra recoiled it, because she was impatient rather than stupid.
They left at first light with a Palace-arranged transport crew, a river passage north, and then a hired mountain caravan for the last six days.
The women called himYoung Masterin front of every one of them.

It came out naturally by the second morning. Seraphine used it flatly, as a title. Vyra used it while handing him a report. Ira managed it with a straight face and a slight delay that only Leon noticed. Loriel used it and then apologized to a boatman for stepping past him, which nobody found strange at all.
The country changed as they went.

The eastern islands gave way to a mainland coast, and the coast gave way to farmland, and the farmland thinned into upland grazing, and by the seventh day the villages had stopped and the road had become a track that a caravan used four times a year. On the ninth day they passed a boundary marker with the Palace’s mark on it and nothing beyond it but grey hills.
The communication windows went through cleanly every second day. Vyra sent them, Han Suwen acknowledged them, and the reports were short and dull and exactly what they should have been.

On the eighth night, they sheltered in a stone waystation while rain drove sideways across the roof. The caravan crew slept beyond a wooden partition, and Seraphine had sealed the household’s half of the room behind a privacy ward before Ira lay on her back and said, "This is the first time."
"First time what," said Vyra.
"That we’ve done this." Ira gestured at the ceiling. "All five of us. Out in the open, going somewhere, and nobody’s hidden in the dimensional world waiting for everyone else to report back."
Nobody answered for a moment.
"Velaria," Seraphine said. "The northern expedition. We travelled with Young Master then."

"That was different and you know it. That was four of us with Young Master somewhere ahead and unreachable." Ira turned her head. "This is the first time I’ve packed a bag for a mission and known I was actually going on it."
Loriel, half asleep against a rolled blanket, said, "I like it."
"That’s because you haven’t had to sleep on stone yet."
"I’ve slept on stone. I planted things in the stone afterward."
Leon lay in the dark and listened to the four of them argue about bedding for another ten minutes, and did not contribute anything, and was as content as he had been since the crossing.
Ashen Rain Basin came up over a ridge on the eleventh day and did not look like a wasteland.
It looked like something that had been hit.

The rim ran in a long shallow curve for as far as Leon could follow it, and inside that curve the ground had been shocked into shapes that ordinary geology did not produce. Shelves of black stone lay across each other in glassy slabs, tilted, fused at the seams. Inside the darker rock, pale branching mineral ran through the stone in forks and forks-of-forks, like something had been frozen mid-strike and then buried.

Steam came up through narrow cracks in eleven places Leon could count from the ridge. There were pools, ringed in mineral crust, some of them faintly steaming and one of them a color he did not have a word for. Hard-leaved plants grew in the lee of the shelves, low and dark and clearly serious about surviving.
Thunder rolled somewhere to the north and kept rolling for eight seconds.

"Stormglass," said Seraphine, quietly. She had crouched at the ridge edge with her hand a few inches above a fused shelf, and had not touched it. "It’s holding a charge. Right now, in the rain, with no lightning nearby."
"Ore under those vents," Vyra said, pointing east. "Look at the color of the crust."
Loriel had already found something growing out of a crack and was refusing to pick it.
"Later," Leon said. "Camp first."
The survey team’s camp sat two hours down the slope, and it was intact.

sentences.text: "Tomorrow morning," said Ji Liansu.
She was already rolling the map.
"You have tonight to prepare, which is less than you want and more than the survey team has.
One thing before you go, and I am not going to repeat the rest of the briefing."
She looked at each of them in turn.
"If you confirm an immortal-level danger, you leave.
If you reach a point where you cannot reliably judge what you are facing, you also leave.
Either condition is enough." Her eyes settled on Leon last.
"You do not remain to verify your conclusion, and you do not stay because retreat would look poor in a report.
Pride has killed more capable people in that basin than lightning has."
"Understood."
Han Suwen laid the equipment out on the table.
Five talismans first, each a folded strip of stiff paper with a jade thread through it, sealed and heavier than paper had any business being.
"Single use.
Anchored to a receiving array under the eastern terrace.
Tear it and you arrive there, wherever you are and whatever is holding you, unless something is actively suppressing space in a way I have never personally seen."
Leon took all five, and then handed them out himself.
He passed one to each woman and watched until all four had secured theirs in separate places.
Vyra raised an eyebrow.
"I could carry them."
"No."
"They’d be organized."
"They’d be in one place," Leon said, "and if that place is separated from the rest of us, four people have no way home." He tucked the last into his own collar.
"Everyone carries their own.
Every day.
Even in camp."
Vyra accepted that without argument and made a note.
The rest followed: the communication plaques, keyed to windows every second day at the third and eleventh marks.
The survey team’s route records and the frequencies their formations had been running.
A map that was excellent for forty kilometers and then showed a blank oval with a hand-inked line around it and the wordsincomplete surveywritten twice.
Sample containers, sealed cases, field supplies.
"Miss a window," Han Suwen said, "and a response leaves within the hour.
That is automatic.
Nobody has to decide it."
They spent the evening preparing, and Leon watched his household turn into a field unit without giving a single instruction.

Vyra had the provisions counted twice and the equipment distributed by weight before the second mark, and then went through the contingencies aloud — what happened if the plaques failed, what happened if they were separated, which of them carried the spare sample seals, and where the reserve stones sat.
Seraphine took the route records and the map to the far end of the table and stayed there for two hours.
When she came back she had a watch order, three rest points chosen for sight lines rather than comfort, and an opinion about how they should move if the storms came in.
"Poor visibility, we go in a stretched diamond," she said.
"Ira forward and left, me forward and right, Leon center, Loriel behind Leon, Vyra rear.
Nobody more than eight paces from two other people.
If we lose sight of each other, everybody stops.
No searching."
"Agreed," said Leon.
Loriel had commandeered a side table and was choosing containers, which turned out to be a considerably longer job than choosing medicines.
"Sealed jade for anything with an active vitality signature," she said, mostly to herself.
"Wood for the dry material.
Nothing in the copper cases — copper leeches.

And I want three empty containers that have never held anything at all, because if there’s something in that basin nobody’s catalogued, I’m not putting it in a jar that spent four years holding blood-lotus."
Ira had been ready in twenty minutes and had spent the two hours since being visibly ready.
"We’re going to a wasteland to look for nine people," she said, on the third pass through Vyra’s contingency list.
"How many ways are there to carry rope."
"Four," said Vyra, without looking up.
"One of which you have chosen, and it is the wrong one, because you have coiled it so it will snag."
"It won’t snag."
"It will snag, and it will snag at the exact moment somebody is hanging from it." Vyra held out a hand.
"Give it here."
Ira gave it over, made a noise of protest that lasted approximately one second, and then leaned over to watch how Vyra recoiled it, because she was impatient rather than stupid.
They left at first light with a Palace-arranged transport crew, a river passage north, and then a hired mountain caravan for the last six days.
The women called himYoung Masterin front of every one of them.
It came out naturally by the second morning.
Seraphine used it flatly, as a title.
Vyra used it while handing him a report.
Ira managed it with a straight face and a slight delay that only Leon noticed.
Loriel used it and then apologized to a boatman for stepping past him, which nobody found strange at all.
The country changed as they went.

The eastern islands gave way to a mainland coast, and the coast gave way to farmland, and the farmland thinned into upland grazing, and by the seventh day the villages had stopped and the road had become a track that a caravan used four times a year.
On the ninth day they passed a boundary marker with the Palace’s mark on it and nothing beyond it but grey hills.
The communication windows went through cleanly every second day.
Vyra sent them, Han Suwen acknowledged them, and the reports were short and dull and exactly what they should have been.
On the eighth night, they sheltered in a stone waystation while rain drove sideways across the roof.
The caravan crew slept beyond a wooden partition, and Seraphine had sealed the household’s half of the room behind a privacy ward before Ira lay on her back and said, "This is the first time."
"First time what," said Vyra.
"That we’ve done this." Ira gestured at the ceiling.
"All five of us.
Out in the open, going somewhere, and nobody’s hidden in the dimensional world waiting for everyone else to report back."
Nobody answered for a moment.
"Velaria," Seraphine said.
"The northern expedition.
We travelled with Young Master then."
"That was different and you know it.
That was four of us with Young Master somewhere ahead and unreachable." Ira turned her head.
"This is the first time I’ve packed a bag for a mission and known I was actually going on it."
Loriel, half asleep against a rolled blanket, said, "I like it."
"That’s because you haven’t had to sleep on stone yet."
"I’ve slept on stone.
I planted things in the stone afterward."
Leon lay in the dark and listened to the four of them argue about bedding for another ten minutes, and did not contribute anything, and was as content as he had been since the crossing.
Ashen Rain Basin came up over a ridge on the eleventh day and did not look like a wasteland.
It looked like something that had been hit.
The rim ran in a long shallow curve for as far as Leon could follow it, and inside that curve the ground had been shocked into shapes that ordinary geology did not produce.
Shelves of black stone lay across each other in glassy slabs, tilted, fused at the seams.
Inside the darker rock, pale branching mineral ran through the stone in forks and forks-of-forks, like something had been frozen mid-strike and then buried.
Steam came up through narrow cracks in eleven places Leon could count from the ridge.
There were pools, ringed in mineral crust, some of them faintly steaming and one of them a color he did not have a word for.
Hard-leaved plants grew in the lee of the shelves, low and dark and clearly serious about surviving.
Thunder rolled somewhere to the north and kept rolling for eight seconds.
"Stormglass," said Seraphine, quietly.
She had crouched at the ridge edge with her hand a few inches above a fused shelf, and had not touched it.
"It’s holding a charge.
Right now, in the rain, with no lightning nearby."
"Ore under those vents," Vyra said, pointing east.
"Look at the color of the crust."

"Later," Leon said.
"Camp first."
